To minimize cyclist fatalities and injuries, effective cyclist warning systems are essential, particularly in scenarios involving motorized traffic and cycling conflicts. While current technologies, such as warning lights and training programs, address specific situations, they lack a comprehensive approach to assessing cyclist risk in diverse environments. In response, this research proposes an innovative cyclist risk inference system, grounded in statistical models, that considers various contextual factors, including road layout, traffic composition, and cyclist behavior. Unlike existing systems, this innovative solution generates a dynamic risk map informed by camera video footage, enabling real-time assessment of cyclist risk and identification of accident-prone cycling routes. Extensive experiments using real-world video data validate the proposed method's efficacy and its potential to significantly enhance the safety of cyclists in diverse settings.

Ensuring the safety and reliability of robots as they navigate through complex environments is crucial, especially when it comes to robots that are in motion. Current safety protocols rely on specific guarantees, where a robot's safe motion is verified by comparing it to a stationary robot's map-based path. However, these protocols fail to account for shifts in the robot's configuration, leading to unsafe conditions when the robot's pose changes. To address this issue, researchers have developed novel methods to securely plan a robot's future movements across its possible configurations. These solutions leverage mathematical principles to ensure that a robot's safe motion across its possible configurations can be guaranteed, even as its pose shifts. By considering the interplay between a robot's pose and configuration, these researchers developed secure navigation algorithms capable of handling dynamic robots in real-world scenarios, where their algorithms successfully ensured the secure traversal of a robot's trajectory across its possible configurations.

Given a ring $R$, its centroid $Z(R)$, an ideal $I(R)$ of symmetric homomorphisms, and a centroid-enveloping number $c(R) = |Z(R)|$, we define the homomorphism-enveloping number $h(R) = |I(R)|$. We establish a formula, $h(R) = c(R)^2$, for semisimple rings $R$ and set a bound, $h(R) \leq c(R)^2$, for any ring $R$ in the process. Furthermore, we identify the condition under which the equality holds, specifically when the centroid is commutative and the ideal $I(R)$ is contained within the centralizer $C_R(R^+) \cap \text{Hom}_\mathbb{Z}(R, R)$. We also show the relationship between the centroid-enveloping number and the maximum idempotent number, $m(R)$, stating that they are equal if and only if the ring $R$ is commutative.

This work successfully achieves robust generalization on Image Classification by training convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with a novel objective function, Robust Objectives. To accomplish this, a CNN is subjected to training on clean images as well as those modified into adversarial examples through an automated process. The level of modification is determined by a parameter within the objective function. As a result, the resulting CNN is anticipated to exhibit resilience against adversarial inputs. To verify this, our CNN is trained on the CIFAR-10 dataset and its performance compared to that of CNNs trained on clean and white-box adversarial datasets respectively. The findings show our model's robust generalization on a test set of adversarial images, with an accuracy surpassing that of the clean-trained model on a dataset contaminated with adversarial images. Moreover, a thorough analysis of our model's robustness is conducted, highlighting its performance on natural adversarial datasets and resistance to adversarial transformations.

We approach singular limit theory for nonlocal traffic models with smooth, data-dependent functions of inter-vehicle distances, under a common set of assumptions. This unifying framework allows us to cover models with symmetric and asymmetric interactions between vehicles. We show that the singular limit of the nonlocal model's solution converges to a nonlocal model describing individual vehicle trajectories as the inter-vehicle distance approach zero. This limit incorporates individual vehicle behaviors such as staying at zero speed, with the model's properties of spatial and temporal conservation of entropy enabling the proof of convergence to a specific type of nonlocal Hamilton-Jacobi equation and its viscous entropy solutions. Furthermore, we show that the rate of convergence can be quantified and improved from a specific to a specific threshold using new estimates. This theoretical framework can be directly applied to a specific car-following model by simply setting a specific parameter.

A complex surface known as a dilation surface can be created by taking a complex surface of finite dilation. The set of closed, non-trivial geodesics on this surface forms a particular structure called an invariant laminations. A method has been developed to prove the existence and uniqueness of this structure on any given dilation surface. The end boundary of this structure on a dilation surface is composed of simple geodesics and is found to be equivalent to the set of core paths of its canonical horizontal lamination, forming a specific link structure. The existence of core links, which are a subset of dilational surfaces, has been discovered in unit quadratic differentials and was previously known to be dense in a particular topological space. The existence of a core link, in turn, guarantees the existence of an invariant lamination on the surface that exhibits Morse-Smale dynamics with respect to the surface's natural dilation surface dynamics, indicating a form of order within the surface's dynamics.

System-wide approaches to the functional connectome of the human brain are crucial for understanding its structure and connectivity. Network metrics like clustering coefficients, connectivity distribution, and hierarchical organization depend on the choice of a specific measure of correlation or association. While traditional methods focus on pairwise relationships, they often overlook complex interdependencies among brain regions. This study introduces an exploratory analysis using a multiple dependence measure known as total correlation. By adapting a rich dataset of 146 individuals' 20-minute fMRI scans into 60-vertex brain parcellations and performing data reduction techniques like random sampling and dimensionality projection, the researchers illustrate how total correlation reveals distinct network topologies. The resulting network metrics, including cluster and small-world characteristics, demonstrate a clear dependence on the data reduction method used, highlighting the necessity of thorough experimentation to produce a specific network structure.

The classical Segal-Bargmann theory explores three key Hilbert spaces of holomorphic functions: one over the complex plane, one composed of polynomials in $2n$ real variables, and one in Clifford algebra-valued polynomials with $2n$ variables. Due to the lack of a universal ordering rule for Clifford algebra elements, these spaces were previously restricted to specific subalgebras where an ordering rule exists (even subalgeges). This paper generalizes Segal-Bargmann theory to all Clifford algebras without specifying a particular basis, defining the Segal-Bargmann transformation as a continuous linear operator between these spaces and without requiring the ordering of algebra elements. We establish that this transformation is an isomorphism and further reveal an unanticipated relationship between Clifford algebra-valued functions and their real-valued counterparts through Taylor isomorphisms. Our work also uncovers significant geometric and algebraic implications.

We have derived a general formula for the conditional distribution of a Gaussian random field based on specific field values from a given path. Our results reveal that Gaussian field conditioning can be understood through a combination of three field components: spatial, temporal, and pathwise. Building upon this insight, we have developed efficient algorithms for computing Gaussian random function conditions, leveraging fast basis expansion models, maximum a posteriori estimation, and sampling methods. To illustrate the utility of our findings, we have applied our approach to a range of problems, including super-resolution, Gaussian process regression, and the study of percolation clusters within the Boolean model.

A future military application will see a drone connect sensors situated on the ground to their peers via a wireless network, facilitating data transfer between non-connected ground sensors and the drone. Each ground sensor must maintain a direct connection to the drone while flying over them at a predetermined altitude, using an antenna with a limited field of view. Only one message per sensor needs to be sent to the drone in any given time slot. We model this scenario mathematically using probability theory, examining the probabilistic coverage of ground sensors by the drone as it moves randomly within a confined area. We derive exact mathematical expressions for the drone's probabilistic coverage of the sensors, average sensor linkage to the drone, and the average number of linked ground sensors, taking into account the drone's height above the ground, its sensor's field of view, the drone's coverage radius, and the total number of ground sensors in the study area. We verify that increasing the drone's coverage radius, its coverage angle, or the drone's altitude results in better sensor linkage, whereas increasing the drone's coverage angle, its coverage radius, or fewer total sensors in the study area leads to a greater probability of sensor linkage.

The DUNE experiment will play a pivotal role in multiple areas of neutrino research, specifically in determining neutrino parameters and related topics, by utilizing long baseline neutrino oscillation analysis. By employing a advanced detector with multiple fine-grained sub-detectors, DUNE will significantly contribute to various scientific fields, including the study of neutrino mass order and potential CP violation phenomena, while also exploring rare processes and neutrino interactions. Furthermore, DUNE will explore astrophysical topics, such as neutrinos originating from supernovae and the Earth's core, ultimately advancing our understanding of these phenomena.

A novel, machine-learning-based approach to enhance top-quark identification has been introduced. The proposed top tagger is composed of three distinct components: a template model that predicts the expected distribution of values for each variable in the classification system, a statistical measure to assess the reliability of using these values to separate top events from W and Z boson events, and a discriminant algorithm that leverages these analyses to create the final tagger. The new top tagger demonstrates improved performance compared to its predecessors, showcasing a 15% to 20% boost in efficiency for both electron and muon-based electrons. The discovery of significant discrepancies in the distribution of key variables for different processes reveals essential insights into the distinct characteristics of quark and lepton jets. The proposed design methodology offers a versatile framework for developing complex algorithms addressing various physics challenges and can be readily applied to substitute more complex algorithms in existing top tagging approaches.

This work proposes an extension to the Virtual Organizational Model (VO) meaning framework, which is based on a refinement framework previously developed in our group. A discussion is presented on VO meaning and refinement, which are essential for defining VO extensions. The approach is tested with two refinement techniques - Composable Adapters and a VO Constructor. We also outline challenges in VO extensions - a key aspect in our research on composable organizations.

A standard technique in model-free reinforcement learning is leveraging past experiences from datasets to stabilize and optimize policy models, known as experience replay. The typical explanation for this approach's effectiveness is the old data's reduced uncertainty, a concept we call variance dimunition. Focusing on the case of the Least-Squares Policy Gradient, we aim to analyze this phenomenon, discovering that the principle can be applied more broadly to other policy optimization methods. Building on this insight, we propose an adaptive experience replay strategy to maximize variance dimunition, which, in experiments, significantly outperforms the standard random replay method across various scenarios.

Superbosonization, an advanced formulation, unifies and broadens various supergaussian and superGaussian identities and their associated formulas, such as the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and super Gaussian exponent decomposition. As a result, it offers a unified framework for expressing superGaussian exponents in diverse ways. Using a simplified example, such as a free super fermion model, the superbosonization equation is demonstrated to be equivalent to both the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and super Gaussian exponent decomposition, and this equivalence extends to apply to more complex scenarios.

In real-world situations, the movements we see around us are interconnected across various dimensions including space, time, and domains like social and geographical areas. To effectively model these complex interactions, existing approaches either focus solely on the temporal aspect or the places where these movements occur, but they are not able to consider both together. This article presents MoDeRNN, a deep learning framework that can capture the spatiotemporal dependencies of a wide range of movement data and accurately forecast future movement states. Building upon an innovative representation of movement data, where each motion aspect is encoded as a latent vector, MoDeRNN incorporates separate Deep RNN modules to learn the spatiotemporal dependencies within each motion aspect. The effectiveness of MoDeRNN has been evaluated through comprehensive experiments conducted on real-world human mobility traces, enabling applications such as future travel time forecasting and travel time cut-off time forecasting in heavy rainfall conditions.

In JavaScript, user input is commonly accessed but can easily trigger security breaches such as reading user passwords. A proposed solution, called Josephines, safely stores such sensitive data within a secure container (a Rust struct) that validates data access through a set of established security rules. These rules ensure that sensitive data in JavaScript can only be used when running within the context of an authentic user. To facilitate this, a bridge is built using WebAssembly to connect the JavaScript and Rust environments, applying the security rules during each method call. To illustrate the concept, we have developed a simulator that allows us to analyze its performance characteristics.

This study investigates the interaction between light and heavy neutral states within the framework of a $10\times 10$ mass matrix under the assumption of type-I seesaw, allowing the researcher to identify an area of interest in the $m_{\beta}-\langle m_\nu \rangle$ plane. The work further explores the correlations between parameters of neutrino oscillation and a combination involving the light neutrino mass parameter and heavy neutrino contributions at colliders for specific values of $\sin^2\theta_{23}$ and $\Delta\textsf{CP}$. A $\sin^2\theta_{23}$ that is non-maximal significantly restricts parameter space, whereas a $\Delta\textsf{CP}$ at CP-conserving levels has a less restrictive impact. Additionally, the research provides a method for inferring the mass spectrum hierarchy and parity assignments of neutral states based on the relationship between parameters $m_{\beta}$ and $\langle m_\nu \rangle$.

Achieving reliable communication over binary erasure channels at minimum possible rates is a long-standing objective in information theory. This goal can be realized by employing a type of error-correction technique known as belief propagation decoding on certain types of codes called low-density parity-check codes. Studies have shown that a subset of codes with a specific subcode structure can essentially replicate the error correction capabilities of random codes. Building upon existing research that identified specific requirements for this type of codes in the large code limit, we have further refined and generalized these findings. Our results not only recover the previous constraints but also remain valid for shorter codes. Moreover, we have explored another type of polar decodable subcodes based on a property discovered in message-passing codes and provided an analysis of their error correction capabilities.

Investigations into combined images of celestial objects have garnered significant interest, particularly regarding uncertainties in their point spread functions (PSFs). These psfs are critical for precision photometry, enabling precise measurements of pixel counts within an object. We have discovered that conventional methods for estimating the psf of a combined image are inaccurate, leading to biased outcomes. We have developed an accurate approach for estimating the psf of a combined image, which is generally narrower than the individual component psfs. We have also identified that the combined psf is influenced by the relative alignment of component images and developed a method to address this issue. Additionally, we have discovered that the combined psf is highly sensitive to variations in the astrometric solutions of component images, which can result in significant uncertainties. We have derived a method to address these variations and minimize the impact on final results.

We utilize the concept of crack tip blunness, when contrasted with a single plane spacing, to derive an expression for a crystal's fracture strength. This is achieved without assuming a particular crack shape. When the fracture strengths of materials with similar bonds but different structures vary by no more than a factor of two, we interpret this as a reflection of the bond's directional nature. In instances where fractures are influenced by flaws, our interpretation holds true. Fracture occurs when the bond's stored energy surpasses the work required for a specific, characteristic movement. In the absence of such a mechanism, the material's fracture strength is dictated by its most robust bond.
A method is outlined for correlating probability measures SLE_n with Gaussian free fields on a polygonal domain whose sides have multiple boundary components.

In this study, we derive precise estimates for the solution of the Navier-Stokes equations with initial data in a particular functional space by constructing a novel norm. This space is defined utilizing the maximum metric from a research paper by H. Shen and T. Wang. Our research shows a significant improvement over existing a priori estimates in comparison with the norms commonly used in literature.

Over the past decade, researchers have extensively studied quantum verification, employing interactive and non-interactive proof systems to enable convincing verification of extremely difficult mathematical problems by untrustworthy sources. This development has led many to view quantum verification as achievable through unreliable sources, but recent research has challenged this view, suggesting that verifying difficult problems requires excessive verification steps. In response, we demonstrate that classical verification of 3-SAT, a particularly complex computational problem, can be achieved in linear time, and we further show that classical verification of quantum circuits, specifically unitary, Clifford, and diagonal circuits, can also be achieved in linear time, and we find that for certain quantum circuit classes, it is possible to create trustworthy verification systems, and we determine the boundaries of this possibility.

A blockchain's inherent security features, like its decentralized structure and immutable ledger, make it a compelling solution for the data storage needs of IoT networks, particularly in sensitive applications like supply chain tracking. While blockchain technology, as exemplified by Bitcoin, was primarily designed for cryptocurrencies and not general data storage due to high costs and limited scalability, more adaptable blockchain alternatives have since emerged. In this paper, we assess the suitability of one such alternative, the Ethereum blockchain, for IoT data storage by highlighting its improved scalability and reduced costs, achieved through the use of oracles and smart contracts. We demonstrate the efficacy of these components in addressing the security challenges of IoT narratives by providing a case study in tamper-proofing the data storage of an emerging IoT application, namely, provenance tracking for data stored in blockchain narratives.

Generative models for creating synthetic cell shapes from training data of existing cells can help scientists study cellular structure variations. Creating diverse, realistic cell shapes is challenging due to the model's ability to represent three-dimensional forms with the freedom to change shape continuously. We develop a new method using neural networks to predict cell shapes. By training with 85 fish embryonic cells, our model can generate over 100 new cell shapes in a consistent and realistic way. To verify our synthetic cells, we compare their shapes to a measurable description of cell forms and calculate the average distances between cells to simulate cell interactions. Our research contributes to understanding cell structure diversity and may help in developing more accurate cell-based models.

Blind individuals often face significant challenges navigating documents due to inadequate table structures and section headings, which make Braille an ineffective solution. Our research on StructureNAPI explores part-document navigability enhancements and introduces a novel technique, IPD-NAV, for improving the navigability of document parts. Our structural NAV approach leverages a neural network to predict a document's structural composition and uses this information to generate navigability improvements. Moreover, IPD-NAV allows for navigability enhancement on a document segment by segment, which is particularly beneficial for documents with varying structures.

Pre-trained language models based on the masked language modeling (MLM) task have achieved significant success, particularly in the case of BERT. Despite its impressive performance, critical aspects of the model remain unclear, raising concerns about its ability to truly learn representations of a language. This research investigates key elements of the MLM formulation, highlighting two main issues: the redundancy of predicting masked context and the inefficiency of using all tokens to fill the gap. To address these limitations, we propose XLNet, pre-training on the new autoregressive task and drawing samples from an augmented set of future and previous tokens in a sequence. Leveraging the autoregressive objective and incorporating novel methods for data sampling, this approach enables a more effective and flexible training process. Experiments conducted on XLNet demonstrate its superiority over BERT on multiple benchmarks, thereby validating the potential benefits of incorporating diverse pre-training tasks.

We studied how stellar activity affects the transmission spectra of exoplanets,
utilizing ground-based observations of the super-Earth WASP-107b. We collected
low-resolution spectra during transit, pre-transit, and post-transit periods,
as well as simultaneous high-resolution spectra with the ESPRESSO spectrograph.
We analyzed these data to compare the transit spectrum, post-transit, and pre-transit
spectra, and detected a large excess in the transit spectrum relative to the
crossed spectra. We found significant differences in the transmission spectrum
across all wavelengths, and estimated the amount of hydroxide in an annular
region to be at least 0.03 M_earth, which is comparable to the hydroxide amount
in an annular region of a comparable planet Earth at its current orbit around the
sun. We replicated the analysis using synthetic observations of active stellar
features and discovered significant differences in the transmission spectrum,
indicating that stellar activity can contaminate transit spectra. However, using
high-resolution spectroscopy allowed us to distinguish exoplanet spectra from
stellar activity, as shown by the close match between the ESPRESSO and low-resolution
post-transit spectra.

For any genus $g\ge1$, we demonstrate that the underlying real line $\mathbb{R}$ can be incorporated into a genus $g$ surface, carrying a projective structure of type IV, where the holonomy type's complexity increases with $g$ for $g>1$.

Our study on the water swimming mechanics of the centipede forficatus using high-speed video analysis and force measurements, revealed that this small (body mass 1.6 micrograms) creature is significantly lighter than previously estimated. Observations showed that for forficatus, swimming at a controllable speed relies on maintaining a balance between thrust and drag forces produced by the legs, with a specific stroke pattern where the water-directed phase lasts twice as long as the recovery phase. A notable finding was that as forficatus loses water-directed muscle control near death, unopposed drag leads to a rapid decrease in swimming speed, ultimately causing it to sink. These results suggest that forficatus relies on previous speed gains to survive rather than controlling its speed, with the water-directed legs acting as a means to delay sinking when food or breathing requirements are met.

Research into the impact of astronomical objects such as asteroids and comets on planets is gaining momentum within the planetary science community. Modeling how these celestial bodies interact with planetary surfaces, and the resulting tsunamis they create, is particularly challenging. From a numerical analysis perspective, the main challenge lies in capturing interactions between air and water phases, and accurately simulating large-scale water movements. In this study, we present initial models for a series of experiments based on a scenario where an asteroid collision occurs on Titan, creating a massive tsunami. We employ a high-resolution method that utilizes adaptive grids and time stepping to track fluid dynamics accurately. By using the Adios-2 code and a multi-block grid system, we have been able to successfully model various aspects of tsunami propagation, including wet-dry boundaries and the interaction between different air and water regions. These simulations demonstrate the potential for high-fidelity, dynamically adjusted numerical models to contribute to our understanding of planetary impacts.

Recent observations of infrared bright galaxies in dense environments have been discovered beyond the local universe. These star-forming galaxies are difficult to detect at optical wavelengths due to severe dust extinction. We have made a comprehensive study of the JADES sample, which comprises 17 galaxy candidates, using the James Webb Space Telescope. By combining optical and near-infrared spectroscopy, we have determined precise redshifts for 15 galaxies, with the highest redshift being $z=2.92$. These galaxies exhibit a wide range of star formation rates from 0.02 to 10 solar masses per year and star formation main sequence values from -2.3 to -0.2. These sources are among the most distant analogues to the JADES-LG, with the exception of two cases, and possess the largest known dust extinctions at early stages of star formation, with dust extinctions ranging from 17 to over 100 magnitudes in the V-band. These extinctions are comparable to those of ultra-luminous infrared galaxies in the local universe. These galaxies are predominantly found in dense environments and exhibit a wide range of metallicities, with dust extinctions being more significant in massive galaxies. These galaxies are found to be significantly more massive than the star formation main sequence, with dust extinctions being lower than in the star formation main sequence. The research delves into four-dimensional topological seven-dimensional supergravity, revealing a profound connection between geometrical components and four-form potential in the bulk. This innovative path leads to a novel formulation where the source of four-form potential in four-dimensional spacetime can be attributed to a seven-dimensional spacetime geometry rather than a seven-brane. This concept is further enhanced by incorporating higher-rank tensors and curvatures in the supergravity action, ultimately yielding terms comprising Riemann curvature, Ricci tensor, and Ricci scalar multiplied by additional fields. Furthermore, a non-minimal coupling between the four-form potential and axion is discovered, resulting in a mathematical framework where the potential's kinetic term emerges as a derivative term due to a mathematical constraint arising from the dual five-form gauge potential boundary condition. This innovative formulation may hold promise for the realization of four-dimensional Riemann curvature terms when combined with other gauge fields, offering a potential new path towards a fundamental theory of string/M-theory.

We investigate the number of configurations for an ensemble consisting of two types of disk masses that can be arranged in an infinite narrow channel. The research builds on the findings of an earlier study by the authors, focusing on arrangements involving only uniform masses. Building upon the previous results, the current study explores alternating sequences between the two sizes and weights of disks, utilizing a mathematical approach based on a hard hexagon model to determine equilibrium coverage fractions and compare them to entropy maximization predictions.

To better understand and forecast extreme precipitation events, we analyzed the distinct effects of differing ENSO flavors on low and high precipitation extremes. ENSO flavors refer to the distinct spatial patterns of sea surface temperature (SST) variability within the ENSO region. Our research shows that Nino4 Heats, characterized by warm SSTs in the central Pacific, strongly influence low precipitation extremes, particularly globally. Conversely, unique El Nino types driven by warm Western Pacific SSTs significantly influence high precipitation extremes, particularly globally. By identifying these distinct effects, we can enhance short-term precipitation forecasts and improve long-term climate modeling to better anticipate extreme climate events in an increasingly warmer world.

The application of external forces to materials with a flexible structure leads to varying responses depending on the magnitude of the force applied. While high forces typically cause uniform deformation across well-solidified materials at low forces applications often result in an uneven deformation process even in materials with high stiffness often referred to as the non-affine deformation regime. Research has been conducted to track these non-affine deformations in materials using optical microscopy. The technique employed involves sending a coherent light beam through a material sample and analyzing the way the light is redirected due to the material's internal structure. The way the light is redirected contains information about the material's local changes. Collecting data over time allows researchers to study how the material grows and understand its growth patterns. A key tool, the structure factor, is often used to quantify the changes in the material's internal structure during deformation. This research aims to develop a population model accounting for demographic and environmental factors, focusing on how waste products impact population dynamics and the effects of age and time delays. Through the development of a single species model with a Leslie type death rate, this study examines the stability and long-term population behavior under varying pollution levels. An mathematical model is constructed and its threshold properties established in terms of a pollution threshold parameter. Additionally, a mathematical model of cellular damage is developed and the threshold for population decline identified. The threshold's influence on population growth rate is also explored through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.

The researchers achieve decidability for an infinite class of substructural logics by using hypersequents, which are formed by combining multiple accessibly related implications. They provide and analyze an exponential-time cut-free sequent calculus, resulting in a paper that offers the first exponential-time sequent calculus for the logic S4d, which is characterized by its contraction and weakening properties. Cut-free sequents serve as a canonical normal form for formulas, enabling the design of a model-checking algorithm for hypersequents and the translation of hypersequents into monosequent systems, with cut-free sequents serving as the basis for the logic. The team also determine the computational complexity of the logic S4d, which is in PSPACE, and establish the undecidability of its superextensions, specifically LS4d and CS4d. They establish and compare the computational complexities of the decidable logics S4d, LS4d, and CS4d to well-known substructural logics, such as the contraction-free logic LK and the contraction-free logic LC, revealing that S4d is the most computationally demanding, followed by LS4d and then LC, with LK being the absolute baseline for computational complexity.

Research has demonstrated the efficacy of neural representation learning in capturing hierarchical concept spaces. However, pre-trained models' manual taxonomy annotations are often laborious and restricted, hindering wide application. To overcome this, research-led products struggle to capitalize on taxonomy growth's potential benefits. An unexpected discovery challenges our assumption that any taxonomy can be effectively modeled using standard representation learning techniques; instead, some taxonomies naturally fit well in non-Euclidean geometric frameworks. Building on this insight, HyperExpan, a novel taxonomy growth framework, leverages hyperbolic representation learning and a specialized HCNN architecture to automatically expand taxonomies. An experimental evaluation using real-world datasets showcases HyperExpan's impressive performance in expanding concepts' meanings and handling large-scale taxonomy growth.

Our research explores the impact of a uniform electric field on various intermolecular forces. By examining multiple pairs of molecules, including those involving noble gases and simple hydrocarbons, within an electric field, we find their interactions remain stable across a wide field range. Furthermore, our findings reveal a systematic relationship between the electric field's effect on molecular interactions and the inherent polarizability of the molecules involved. Notably, our research demonstrates that quaternary complexes can exhibit stable configurations due to electric field-induced interactions, supported by our calculated equilibrium arrangements. Our results also reveal a distinct pattern in the electric dipole potential created by molecular pairs, which can be used to explain the stabilization of complex structures in the presence of an electric field. Additionally, our research shows the existence of a specific arrangement within quaternary complexes, in which the electric field's influence is minimized, effectively neutralizing the effects of the electric field. The findings presented in this research have significant implications for the study of biological processes, as well as for the development of advanced materials and molecular materials. Our research highlights the importance of considering the electric field's effect on molecular interactions, particularly for the study of biological processes and the design of advanced materials and molecular materials. The fourth Industrial Revolution brings substantial digital transformation opportunities to manufacturing systems capable of handling non-deterministic operations, like batch processing, which inherently involve unpredictable outcomes. By leveraging Industry 4.0 technologies and advanced scheduling techniques for smart and flexible manufacturing, outcomes can be predicted and optimized, despite their non-deterministic nature. To address this, our paper outlines a comprehensive framework scheduling approach, incorporating uncertainty-aware models for resource consumption and batch processing tasks. We contrast our method with a baseline deterministic model in terms of completion time and predictive accuracy. An application case in the pharmaceutical industry illustrates the framework's practicality and effectiveness.

In this research, a framework for evaluating the robustness of Cyber-Physical Systems via temporal logic is established. Formulated in STL, a new definition of resilience is stated, and and-dualness properties are utilized to simplify calculations. Furthermore, a method for transforming discrete CSP models into robustness values, accompanied by an optimization technique to maximize resilience, has been developed. The proposed approach has been successfully applied to both a logical example and a more complex SMR motor vehicle model.

A new approach to detecting dark matter via pulsar timing has been introduced by combining the data from timing arrays with those from interplanetary accelerator networks. Accelerometer data can reveal dark matter structure on a scale of astronomical units, complementing the data from pulsar timing arrays at sub-asteriscal scales. Two analysis techniques have been proposed to estimate the dark matter structure power spectrum from accelerator data, along with a simulation of such a network's behavior. It was found that this network can detect sub-asteriscal dark matter fluctuations up to frequencies of 1 cycle per month and that data from multiple networks can provide a three-dimensional map of dark matter fluctuations. Accelerometer networks offer a cost-effective and versatile means to constrain dark matter fluctuations at infrequent frequencies, complementing the capabilities of pulsar timing arrays.

Consider a nonlinear diffusion equation on a complete manifold M with given equation parameters and conditions, where the manifold has either non-negative or non-positive Ricci curvature. In the case of non-negative Ricci curvature, we derive an estimate for the solution with sub-Ricci curvature bounded from below, assuming the initial solution has bounded support. Conversely, in complete manifolds with non-positive Ricci curvature, we establish an estimate for the solution with initial bounded support in terms of the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator. Furthermore, in the case of bounded initial solution, we obtain a lower bound for the solution in terms of the manifold's isoperimetric profile.

The sources discussed in this study are single, isolated low-frequency radio waves originating from the sources z=0.1-0.6 at a frequency of 140 MHz. By employing a stacking technique, the average morphology of these low-signal sources is examined in terms of angular size, brightness distribution, surface brightness, and edge brightness. Our analysis reveals that these low-signal sources display a bright core with diffuse and faint extended lobes, exhibiting asymmetry. Additionally, we derived that these low-signal sources have angular sizes of 1.3' $\pm$ 0.1', being fainter than their core regions and exhibiting higher brightness near their core. We also found edge brightness to be higher than their surface brightness, with both parameters increasing as the source becomes fainter.

This paper introduces the concept of (Quantitative) Information Flow as an extension of Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and interprets the observation process as a monadic fold. To accommodate both discrete and continuous time frames, we expand discrete HMMs to a time-frame-independent form and further develop an observation monad for this generalization. To represent the real-valued probabilities inherent in continuous systems, we introduce a Continual HMM, which is specifically described using a categorical framework and characterized by a monadic interface. Our approach to *continual HMMs* is a formal set of axioms, which is then applied to describe a category of functors serving as a continuous HMM framework. This framework is subsequently used to interpret quantitative information flow on both a quantitative flow category and a function category for measuring information leakage. By doing so, we demonstrate that the level of information leaked between a system's history and time frame is equivalent to the mutual information between those entities.

Nonlocal-in-space models effectively capture crucial phenomena like turbulence and shock waves. However, the question arises as to why the same nonlocal-in-space concept appears in multiple physical systems. We demonstrate that turbulence and dynamically consistent structures such as jets and wakes exhibit the same nonlocal-in-space characteristics due to an underlying general principle. Specifically, we show that a broad category of deterministic and stochastic nonlocal-in-space models can be derived from a single universal formula based on the Fourier transform of the wavelet associated with the flow's homogeneous components. As a result, we develop a new statistical nonlocal-in-space model representing jets and waves and provide an explicit formula for the associated wavelet, along with theoretical and numerical evidence for its validity.

We introduce a versatile framework to scatter arbitrary numbers of particles in various spaces dimensions and spins. The method can adapt to multiple channels, allowing particles to transition between them, each with its own mass shell constraints. The algorithm's core lies in using recursion relations to build up binary interaction building blocks into more complex amplitudes across these channels. This framework encompasses multiple particle spins and is also capable of handling fixed shells constraints across different channels. As applications, we compute scattering probabilities for particles with high spins up to rank 3, and for interactions in spaces dimensions up to 6. Additionally, we extend the standard gravity and scalar gravity amplitudes calculations by incorporating shells constraints across two channels. Specifically, we calculate two gravitons scattering amplitude under the constraint that one outgoing particle has an extra mass shell constraint (1/2 more mass), yielding two new basis elements in four dimensions. A similar computation is performed for two scalons amplitude with one shell constraint for φ^4 theory in various dimensions.

We've mathematically modified the blackbody radiation energy density, taking into account the impact of Casimir's influence. Building upon the Planck distribution, our work considers how modulating the space affects radiation, yielding a modified density. Under specific boundary conditions, our results demonstrate a shift from one type of force to another. A potential application involves the development of an innovative energy source, powered by the transition between attractive and repulsive Casimir forces.

This work focuses on establishing a foundational framework for evaluating the confidentiality of location tracks, considering a broader range of considerations beyond existing methods. We begin by reviewing the principles of differential privacy and conditional differential privacy, identifying their shortcomings in this context. The proposed framework comprises two critical components: the conditional distribution of location tracks, given prior knowledge of specific locations and an initial prior estimate, which influences data influence. To facilitate a comprehensive evaluation, we suggest considering additional factors, including the impact of this estimate on data influence, prior knowledge of data subjects, and the effect of this knowledge on data influence. Based on this, we introduce a new concept called the conditional prior privacy of location tracks, which synthesizes the above considerations. We demonstrate the relationship between this concept and differential privacy, and introduce new properties that generalize differential privacy for this context. Furthermore, we introduce two mechanisms that enable the application of a composition mechanism to preserve conditional prior privacy.

The 3D point cloud localization method utilizing the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation has gained popularity due to its effectiveness. However, traditional localization algorithms based on NDT focus on real-time processing and are thus restricted to small search ranges. To overcome this limitation, a new proposed method integrates the capabilities of the transformer architecture with NDT features, enabling search within a large global map. Our method achieves a precise NDT localization accuracy of 7.4cm and can locate the pose within a 2m x 2m search range. Experiments conducted on the KITTI dataset demonstrate that it outperforms a state-of-the-art method by attaining higher accuracy and more rapid convergence times.

Research has shown that functional MRI can identify distinct neurological disorders, but this application relies on the predictive power of the technique, which remains uncertain due to a lack of theoretical understanding of its noise properties. We analyzed fMRI connectivity patterns across multiple brain regions, revealing consistent structures within individual brains despite a lack of visible signal in the data. This suggests that there is a underlying functional connection between distant brain regions, but this connection weakens with increasing distance between the regions. We also established a baseline of variability in healthy brains, which serves as a reference point for evaluating how well a neural network model can accurately predict a person's health. Using this framework, we found that the most predictive neural networks tend to connect brain regions that play similar roles across different brain systems, regardless of their spatial location within the brain. This indicates that inter-individual variations in connectivity patterns are not only common, but are also highly structured and reliable.

We investigate the time complexity of the naming problem within energy-efficient networks consisting of nodes with transmission and reception capabilities but lacking processing power and storage. This energy-efficient model operates under specific constraints where transmitted signals persist for an extended period and consume the same amount of energy whether active or not. Our focus is on a highly restricted communication model where processing units are absent, and we develop two recursive algorithms, relying on random transmission times and dictionary-word transmission, to achieve efficient node identification. Specifically, we devise an $O(n^2)$-algorithm for nodes with long-range transmission lines and create an $O(2^n)$-algorithm for nodes that can only receive or transmit '1' values. Furthermore, we devise an $O(n^2)$-algorithm for nodes capable of transmitting '0' lines, complemented by a lower bound of $n-1$ for any naming scheme in this context.

This paper investigates the multilingual characteristics of Code-Mixed Text, a form in which words or sentences are combined from two or more languages in a seamless manner. Our approach, Code-Mixed Language Positional Encoding (CMLE), employs a technique that uses fixed-position switching points to interchangeably arrange words from both languages in a unified representation of the input sentence. Our experiments, conducted on four code-mixed datasets (Hindi-Mix, Urdu-Mix, Tamil-Tanglish, and Telugu-Teluglish), demonstrate that our method yields superior results compared to a basic positional encoding technique and a relative positionally encoded BERT model, outperforming the state-of-the-art models by margin. Additionally, a systematic analysis of our method reveals its efficacy in achieving comparable performance to domain-adapted models without the need for additional training.

Using a combination of ab-initio calculations of density functional theory and a detailed analysis of time-dependent mean-field Hartree-Fock theory, we've examined the structural, electronic and superconducting properties of H$_3$S under high pressure, specifically in the Fm$\bar{3}m$ phase where superconductivity peaks at room temperature. We've found significant enhancements in superconductivity near the van Hove singularity, peaking at a pressure of 223 GPa, near which we've observed a steep rise in superconducting gap parameters, particularly the d-wave gap. Notably, our analysis reveals a negative isotope effect in this vicinity due to a combination of electronic and phonon characteristics. Isotope sensitivity analysis indicates a strong influence of light isotopes at low temperatures, transitioning to an equal-superconducting-gap behavior at higher temperatures, ultimately resulting in an equal isotope effect.

Most motion planning algorithms struggle to operate efficiently in environments with dynamic obstacles. Tradging off the environment's representation, higher dimensionality allows for more accurate motion planning, particularly for systems constrained by restriction curves. Our novel method generates restriction curves that are both compact and suitable for planning, capable of modeling dynamic obstacles without increasing complexity. To achieve this, we represent the movement of such obstacles as a series of curves, allowing for a unified approach to motion planning. Our method draws inspiration from grid-based approaches but replaces grid constraints with continuous curves, preserving computational efficiency. We combine these curves into a filter, eliminating curves that do not intersect with the configuration space obstacle boundary, resulting in a subset of restriction curves that can be used for motion planning. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through comparison with grid-based planning on a dynamic robot motion model.

Visual localisation is a critical component of many robotic systems that relies heavily on accurately identifying a camera's position. Two main approaches to visual localisation, local and global, have been developed. Local localisation involves low-computation tasks like batch processing, matching features, or performing iterative optimisation. In contrast, global localisation with visual localisation (VVL) requires solving a computationally challenging problem: determining which pose best matches a camera's features against a pre-built 3D map, which is often based on various sensors. This process typically demands significant computational power and extensive map descriptors. 3D surface elements (surfels) present an effective solution by effectively matching features against complex scenes and can be built up over time. This paper presents a vVL method, which employs learned surfel-based 3D maps for robust visual localisation across various environments. By using surfel-based 3D maps constructed from multiple views, our approach can perform both local and global localisation. These surfel-based maps, which can be continuously updated, are shown to improve visual localisation performance, particularly when dealing with cameras that have limited fields of view.

In Multi-Input Multi-Output systems, the simultaneous selection of users and design of precoding vectors poses significant challenges due to the problem's non-convex and combinatorial nature. 
A new approach based on the Group LASSO method has been proposed, which reformulates the problem as a convex one that can be efficiently solved using an alternating optimization technique. 
To ensure that user choice remains invariant during the precoder design process, the proposed approach incorporates historical data on user selection. 
To further enhance performance in high Signal-to-Noise Ratio conditions, the proposed approach also demonstrates an asymptotic equivalence with the LASSO method, which can yield superior performance. 
In order to track users' movement over time, the proposed approach utilizes the LASSO solution from the previous time slot as a starting point for the current slot. 
Simulation results demonstrate the proposed approach's high performance in the initial phase and its ability to maintain performance on par with the LASSO method in dynamic user scenarios.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve is generated by a finite set of rational functions. This result implies that the rational and regular semirings of tropical curves are finitely generated. Moreover, the rational function semifield possesses specific structural characteristics such as being maximally embedded in the order valuation of rational functions and possessing a specific type of basis system, known as a weak Noetherian apparatus. These characteristics along with rational function properties enable the tropical analogues of the Riemann-Schottky problem and the Brill-Noether theorem to be formulated.

In binary classification, the quality of any classifier is quantified by its excess risk, a metric that measures its deviation from the optimal Bayes classifier's risk.  We present a condition, more lenient than that traditionally used, under which an estimator of the classifier's Q-function converges uniformly to the true Q-function with high probability.  This result is significant because it demonstrates that empirical risk minimization can yield a classifier that minimizes the excess risk across a range of possible functions.  We apply our finding to a class of estimators known as partitioning rules, for which we establish convergence rate bounds.  Furthermore, we use these new techniques to re-examine existing estimators, including the Probit-Averaging Algorithm, allowing us to better understand its performance characteristics and derive novel rate bounds for this estimator.

A key component in a proof that 3-dimensional open manifolds have nonnegative torsion is the Fox-Hatcher loop, constructed from a spanning surface of the manifold. In our study, we calculate the Fox-Hatcher loop with respect to three-dimensional and pure 3-variable Vassiliev invariants that have local support near a single point. Additionally, we derive a calculable form for a specific Vassiliev invariant by linking it to a related function of braids and by computing its Lagrangian signature contribution.

The connection between superconductivity and nematic order, particularly in systems where nematic order nearly occurs, can provide significant insights into the orbital superconductivity puzzle. This connection was particularly prominent in systems like Ba1-xAxAs2 and Sr1-xCx2As2, which undergo a structural phase transition at finite temperatures that is suppressed by superconductivity. However, in other iron-based superconductors such as Co-doped LiFeAs, the structural phase transition does not occur, yet it appears to be close to a critical point. In an attempt to understand the relationship between these two orders in this system, we conducted a comprehensive study using the LDA+DoC method to investigate how non-equilibrium fluctuations influence the system's properties and superconductivity in the absence of a finite-temperature phase transition. Our results show that nematic and spin-fluctuation instabilities coexist in LiFeAs, with superconductivity being driven primarily by spin fluctuations. This, combined with evidence that superconducting gaps in LiFeAs are sensitive to changes in lattice parameters, indicates that the structural phase transition in LiFeAs is close to a critical point but that nematic order has not emerged.

We investigate results from a Type-II two-Higgs-doublet model with an updated global fit, taking into account current constraints on Higgs coupling strengths, mass limits for additional Higgs bosons from LHC searches, and precise measurements of Z and W boson properties consistent with the Standard Model prediction. Although previous studies found a non-zero upper limit on the heavy Higgs boson coupling $\xi_{\text{h}}$ and predicted an upper mass bound of around 1 TeV for $\text{H}^+$, our analysis reveals that in the absence of a light CP-odd Higgs boson mass limit, $\xi_{\text{h}}$ can reach non-negligible values and $\text{H}^+$ may have a mass above 1 TeV. Our results contradict earlier predictions. On the other hand, our results align with those from a more comprehensive 2HDM framework that includes the supersymmetric Standard Model as a special case.

We aim to investigate particle-based simulation capabilities trained using neuroevolutionary methods to identify promising configurations for assembly tasks. Through genetic algorithms, we develop and evolve strategies for optimizing particle arrangements. To facilitate this, we create a versatile generative model for simulation particles and assembly structures using tensors, and we implement neural control and optimization techniques, including reinforcement learning and Monte Carlo tree search, to train our models. As a result, we create complex molecular shapes, including molecules with the shape of letters, and we discover effective placements of emitters to steer gas particles into desired configurations.

Our anomaly analysis and robust analysis confirm the chiral phase diagram we previously proposed, expanding on our initial findings with more thorough theoretical justification. A key finding in our research is the necessity for Dirac fermions in two of the models, resulting in specific symmetries, while another is constrained by chiral global anomalies. Notably, the theory with $SU(N)_{\gamma}$ global anomaly has no realizable representation. This work supplements our prior study, which explored the theory's properties in the context of a massless fermion gas.

This study examines the behavior of the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in a specific mathematical framework involving periodic three-dimensional functions. We demonstrate that there is no unique solution starting from specific initial conditions when the starting conditions meet certain minimal irregularity requirements. To address this issue, we explore whether local regularizing effects within the solution equation can establish additional constraints on initial conditions to ensure unique solutions. We show this regularizing influence does not hold, via a specific counterexample where we find initial conditions with optimal critical scaling that maintain their specific class within an approximate zero solution with minimal irregularity for any positive time period. We achieve this through a novel approach where we use trigonometric polynomial projections as essential tools for the analysis.

We've explored how the interaction between magnons in antiferromagnetic materials changes with the temperature generated by these magnons. Our research is based on a quantum field theoretical model that describes this interaction through a non-linear interaction involving three magnons. Using an approach called the thermal dressed Hamiltonian, we've been able to calculate key properties,50,60,69,75 including the non-linear spectral shift experienced by magnons and their thermal self-energy. We've found that this interaction becomes stronger as the temperature increases, potentially affecting the stability of these magnons. Our results also show significant changes in the magnons' frequency and can lead to them becoming unstable under high temperatures. Our predictions align with experimental findings obtained through neutron scattering techniques. Our research provides valuable insights derived from precise measurements, reinforcing our understanding that this interaction plays a crucial role in magnons within antiferromagnetic materials.

Loidreau's LSE code-based cryptosystem, which is an extension of the Reed-Muller scheme similar to the GRS codes, poses a challenge in its mathematical representation due to a known quasi-systematic structure that risks compromising security. To overcome this issue, Loidreau employed a random affine transformation on the input and output spaces, but this was only partially effective in concealing the code's structure. Our research reveals two novel approaches to mask the inherent structure of LSE codes more effectively. Firstly, analogous to the method used in LC-MD, we apply an alternative LSE code construction utilizing a non-linear map from a larger finite field to a smaller one. This newly employed method offers enhanced resistance to attacks by breaking the quasi-systematic structure while also allowing for a greater number of secret parities and a larger code size without a corresponding increase in penalty. Secondly, we implement a random linear map instead of an affine transformation on the input space, thereby eliminating the code's quasi-systematic structure.

Language models pre-trained using methods like masked language modeling are typically trained on vast datasets of unstructured text. These models are expected to learn word relationships from a limited amount of training data. To address a key challenge - the one-to-many mapping problem - we suggest incorporating the benefits of a comprehensive thesaurus into the pre-training process. By utilizing the thesaurus, we can group similar words, providing the model with clearer relationships between these words. Our proposed method combines this idea with self-supervised learning in a new pre-training task called consistent masked language modeling. We tested this approach on the BERT model and found through ablation studies that our method successfully addresses the word similarity issue and leads to better model performance when evaluated using a benchmark suite of tasks.

We investigate the behavior of certain random structures as their size increases without limit by using filters, such as persistence diagrams, to analyze their properties. We consider two specific models: a random complex (a 2-dimensional structure) and the Erdos-Renyi random graph, and we examine the mass of the minimal spanning acyclic diagrams resulting from sampling these models with various degrees and p, respectively. Our analysis reveals that the mass of this diagram converges to a specific value, and we can characterize this convergence mathematically by using the degree distribution function and the edge probability p, respectively. Our results also show that the limiting value is the same for models with finite second moment degree distributions and graph models with exponentially decaying probabilities for high-degree nodes.

Federated learning is a groundbreaking technique for training machine learning models while preserving data integrity. A novel approach, vertical federated vertical learning, has further enhanced data confidentiality in specific contexts. To evaluate security in this context, researchers developed two new attacks: a localized version of the curve-fitting attack and a data-fragmentation attack. Researchers implemented these attacks in both a game and a real-world setting to assess their effectiveness. Notably, when attacking fragmented data, the accuracy of reconstructed patient records from insurance companies' records achieved an impressive 85% recall rate, demonstrating the potential vulnerabilities of this federated learning protocol.

We investigate the decay processes of $B$-mesons that result in a proton and an dark antibaryon through the light cone sum rules method. This method necessitates a non-zero value of the coupling constant between the dark baryon and the standard model, specifically $\langle p | \bar{\psi}_\psi \psi_q | n \rangle \equiv \beta$. Our analysis leverages QCD light cone sum rules to determine $\beta$ for a given proton structure function $C_2^p(x_B, Q^2)$, ultimately allowing for the calculation of the branching ratio for the decay $B \to P D_{baryon} D^\dagger_{antibaryon}$. This Shapiro-Wilks $W_0$ statistic was used to assess the significance of $C_2^p(x_B, Q^2)$ variability in relation to $\beta$ at a 95% confidence level. Utilizing the best-fit $\beta$ value, our study reveals a correlation between $C_2^p(x_B, Q^2)$ and the upper limit of the branching ratio for $B \to D_{baryon} D^\dagger_{antibaryon}$.
