Research has shown high-quality approximations of the Schrodinger equation for a large class of weakly and rapidly oscillating complex Hamiltonians with frequencies. We explore and provide exact high-frequency expansions for Lindblad equations with the same oscillating properties, which also apply to certain Lindbladians, including frequency- and time-independent cases. Our findings demonstrate that these expansions can be used to address global existence problems, which we demonstrate through generating functionals for sub-Markovian semigroups. An example is given where the existence of a solution to the Lindblad equation for all times is established by choosing a weak oscillation frequency and a non-resonant driving frequency in a system of two coupled two-level systems.

Our recent studies of the effect of rhodium substitution in the CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ series revealed that while ferromagnetic ordering occurs at low rhodium concentrations, it transitions to nonmagnetic states at higher rhodium concentrations, as confirmed by specific heat and $\mu$SR measurements. Neutron inelastic scattering measurements showed that ferromagnetic ordering persists up to high rhodium concentrations but beyond x = 0.1 it de-polarizes the neutron beam. By utilizing a polarization analysis, we were able to determine that this depolarization is due to the magnetic moment being randomly oriented in the plane perpendicular to the neutron beam. Depolarization begins at x = 0.12 and reaches a point where magnetic moments are completely perpendicular to the neutron beam at x = 0.2. Moreover, our results indicate that magnetic fluctuations measured in experiments depend on both the magnitude of the magnetic moments and their orientation relative to the neutron beam. These findings highlight an essential consideration in neutron scattering measurements of samples with in-plane magnetic moments.

Scientists have recently identified an extremely dense molecular cloud, named G176.51+00.20, which is characterized by its extremely high electron density and high electron temperature. This research aims to explore the formation of massive stars within this cloud, which exhibits notable H I narrow-line emissions. Using a C-Band radiotelescope, researchers have detected these emissions and investigated their scientific implications. The observed features of these emissions indicate that they originate from collisions, and their excitation conditions are analyzed in relation to self-emission. This research reveals that the collisional processes are primarily responsible for the formation of these emissions and that their intensity is directly related to the electron density within the cloud. Additionally, researchers have discovered that electron-ion collisions play a crucial role in the thermal equilibrium of the electrons, and the formation of these emissions is primarily influenced by the electron density within the cloud.

We characterize certain beta-transformations such that for a particular set of intervals with a single hole, the invariant measures have a specific single-peak density across each interval. This implies that these beta-transformations may be thought of as acting similarly to certain greedy beta-transformations with a single hole, and thus have the same effect on beta-transformations acting on a more complex set.

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s from the CP-violating differences between CP-odd and even initial states in Bs decays can provide insights beyond the Standard Model. Our analysis involves measuring phi_s in Bs decays to J^+/π^- and J^-/π^+, J^+/ρ^- and J^-/ρ^+, where J^+/π^+ decays are dominated by longitudinal polarization, allowing a more accurate measurement of phi_s that accounts for small admixtures of unpolarized states. Our data from 19.3 fb^-1 of pp collision events at a centre-of-mass energy of 8 TeV, collected by the LHCb experiment, yields a measurement of phi_s = 0.004 ± 0.030 (stat.) ± 0.119 (sys.) rad. This is the first phi_s determination involving hadronic final states and currently offers the most precise phi_s measurement overall.

This study investigates domain adaptation methods for enhancing the performance of a deep neural network when it is trained on limited data from an unfamiliar test environment. We utilize two representative computer vision applications, both of which are well-documented in existing literature, to evaluate these methods. The first is a facial recognition dataset consisting of 10 deep feature embeddings per person from 10 distinct deep neural networks, our secondary objective being the comparison of our results with prior studies on cross-database face recognition. The second is colorization, a task involving the conversion of grayscale images into full color representations, where neural networks are trained to map colorized pixels from a specific dataset. The effectiveness of these methods is evaluated using three evaluation metrics, which are calculated on unseen test datasets. The evaluation reveals that training the deep neural network using a combination of representative samples from multiple domains, combined with random re-sampling, yields the best performance when applied to both face recognition and colorization tasks.

For any 2-dimensional vector space over a finite field F_q and a function f in that space, we examine the set of curves that have a node at a specified point and tangency with a tangent in a particular direction, with the purpose of determining how many such curves exist and predicting a bound based on the number of points of a certain type and a particular exponent in an inequality related to the number of points.

A visual demonstration of the Bell numbers is provided through a tetrahedral structure, and the accompanying illustrations offer an explanatory evidence of the underlying theorems: the summation formula, the recursive equation, and the summation identity.

This paper proposes an abstract graph representation called a Graph Representation Abstract Machine (GRAM) to describe the computational process of a family of graph neural network (GNN) models. We designed GRAM as a parameterized interpreter that can execute any GNN model by configuring it with the relevant GNN model structure and associated parameters. Our study evaluates four typical GNN metrics on three benchmark datasets, comparing them to our new method that utilizes GNN models as libraries instead of traditional GNN models trained directly. Our findings demonstrate that our approach can achieve competitive results while offering explainability, efficient memory usage, and easy model modification capabilities.

We analyzed the Subaru Broad Band Optical Survey's new galaxy cluster, RXCJ03:42-4420, to investigate its substructures. By examining the galaxies within and around the cluster, we located a previously unknown companion cluster at approximately 3.5 degrees away. This system comprises a primary cluster with a velocity dispersion of 1060 km/s and a secondary cluster at a relative distance of about 1000 km/s. The research also revealed a group of galaxies between the main and secondary clusters moving at around 400 km/s. Furthermore, the presence of a fourth galaxy group was suggested, possibly indicating a four-cluster system. By combining X-ray data and a galaxy redshift survey, a rich galaxy cluster was found, also located approximately 3.5 degrees away. This system contains a massive galaxy cluster with a mass of approximately $1.25 \pm 0.10 \times 10^{14} M_{\odot}$. The research also examined the morphological properties of galaxies within and around the cluster, indicating a preference for red, elliptical, and elliptical-shaped galaxies within the cluster. Additionally, the research found that galaxies within and around the cluster exhibit minimal substructure, with no obvious signs of a recent merger event, with a merging timespan of approximately 1.5 billion years.

The Legendre Memory Block (LMB), a transformer-free, high-performance architecture, has its training process limited by an inefficient memory and a sequential nature. To address this, a parallelized memory entropization approach is introduced, leveraging a relaxation method to optimize computation. The proposed solution reduces the processing time for memory parameter optimization and is supported by detailed complexity analysis, as well as empirical validation of its efficiency method.

In recent years, particle physics experiments have shown a heightened enthusiasm,
driven by recent findings that have significantly altered past perspectives.
A particular area of interest involves feeblely-interacting particles predicted
by theoretical frameworks beyond the Standard Model, specifically its dark matter
variant. Research into such particles faces particular challenges, necessitating
the development of increasingly sophisticated and sensitive experimental tools.
This article provides a comprehensive review of the current research landscape,
detailing the innovative experiments that have been conducted over the past
decade, with an emphasis on next-generation projects poised to reveal new
insights in the coming years.

The widespread use of multiple language labels for various concepts is a known issue, creating difficulties for communication between individuals and systems using different languages. In an effort to understand how a single, unified vocabulary can emerge, we investigate a naming game where words are continuously exchanged among a population of migrating individuals within a semi-regular network structure. Focusing on a two-word scenario with three possible labels, we uncover a self-organizing mechanism that facilitates the development of a single dominant label across large portions of the network. We derive both theoretical and numerical results that reveal how this emergence occurs over a broad range of gene migration rates.

Deep learning's application in physics is gaining momentum due to its potential in numerical approximation, yet determining the optimal training strategy for such applications remains unclear. This study examines the impact of incorporating momentum during gradient descent training on physics-informed neural networks' ability to learn solutions to differential equations. By investigating the role of a common form of bias in these models, which influences learning behavior, this research finds that incorporating momentum during training can counteract this bias. As a result, these models can be trained more effectively with less data and provide more accurate approximations, even in complex, non-convex problems, which is a significant finding. The implications of these results are far-reaching, allowing for the use of PNNs in a range of complex, real-world problems without extensive pre-processing or computational resources.

We examine a two-wave system in a bounded domain under Kelvin-Voigt dissipation applied in limited areas, in conjunction with coupling damping and control. The first equation adheres to Kelvin-Voigt dissipation, while the second follows waves with control, allowing the use of a regularity transfer function. This is achieved through a transposition method, where an exact boundary observability inequality is first established for the second wave. A key step involves constructing a "cut and paste" test function that accounts for the reduced regularity of the adjoint state, allowing for a stability proof for the coupled system.

Deep Reinforcement Learning has proven highly effective in navigating complex environments, yet it often lacks transparency in its learned behaviors, a problem that can be critical when implementing actions in the real world. Furthermore, deep reinforcement learning models frequently struggle to accurately predict outcomes in untested situations. To address these limitations, we've developed an innovative, transparent model-based reinforcement learning approach, leveraging inductive logic programming, without relying on a pre-defined system model. Our approach allows the learning agent to concurrently learn a interpretable system model, which enables the safe application of hierarchical planning methods like GTNF. We've also presented an algorithm for inducing logic rules directly from first-order labels produced by MDPs, a previously unexplored application of inductive logic programming. Experimental results using classic control tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding improved performance and a increased understanding of the agent's learned behaviors, particularly in environments with partial model observations, where we've found that our method is more similar to the true environment dynamics compared to traditional reinforcement learning methods.

Asymmetric behavior has garnered significant attention in various fields, particularly in nonlinear optics, due to its numerous applications and inherent significance. Breaking optical symmetry is crucial for inducing unidirectionality and asymmetric coupling. Recent studies have focused on optical asymmetry induced by electromagnetic诱导 transparency in nonlinear media through continuous wave laser interaction, as well as asymmetry generated by mode coupling in multi-waveguide systems. However, researchers have not extensively explored the possibility of quantum noise-induced optical asymmetry. In this study, we demonstrate that optical asymmetry can be generated by quantum fluctuations in a two-type two-level atom system doped in a photonic crystal fiber, subjected to a specially configured three-frequency electromagnetic field featuring a strong control field, a weak probe field, and a Stokes field with a moderate frequency. The key to achieving this asymmetry lies in manipulating the cross-correlated quantum fluctuations between the Stokes and anti-Stokes fields in the system's Heisenberg-Langevin equations. Furthermore, adjusting the probe field's detuning and the control field's detuning enables the introduction of various damping terms in the equations of motion for the probe field's steady-state field amplitude and one-photon coherence, thereby allowing for control over optical asymmetry. Additionally, our findings affirm the feasibility of detecting this asymmetry through electromagnetic nonlinearity.

Let $h$ be a $2\pi$-periodic function expressed as a finite complex Fourier series with real coefficients $h_k$, and consider the function $H(x) = \sum_{k=1}^N h(kx)$ defined on the torus $\mathbb{T}^N$ where $h(kx)$ denotes the Fourier extension of $h$ to $\mathbb{T}^1$. This study investigates a variational problem by finding functions $h_k$ that minimize a certain expression $J$, subject to the constraint $\int_{\mathbb{T}^N} H(x)dx = 0$. As the number of terms $N$ approaches infinity, we prove that $J$ converges towards the supremum of the expression $\sup_{\phi \in \mathcal{P}} \int_{\mathbb{T}^N} \Phi(H(x) + \phi)dx$ with $\Phi$ being a convex function and $\phi$ being any function in $\mathbb{T}^N$ and $\mathcal{P}$ the set of all convex functions with a non-negative derivative. Finally, we apply our result to particular functions such as $\Phi(u) = \max(0, u)^p$ and $\Phi(u) = \sqrt{1+u^2}$.

Our investigation into rapidly rotating $^6$Li as a means to detect shadow dark matter focuses on its strong dependence on the spin of its components. Our spin-dependent cross-section analysis with $^6$Li, which can be carried out using a neutron detector, is expected to have a $5\sigma$ signal within one year's worth of data, with an energy threshold of 3.5 keV. Our predictions also surpass those of traditional proton-based targets in their ability to detect shadow dark matter with m$_{\chi}$ values of less than ~1 GeV.

A groundbreaking approach to single-image blind deblurring and image denoising has emerged as the primary focus of contemporary image processing research, where previously independent blurring and noise models are now unified into a single framework for enhanced efficiency. Building on a previous generalization of the blur model that incorporated the Mixture of Experts model (MoE), this work extends the framework to account for the blurring of blurred and noiseless images, as well as their corresponding noise conditions, thereby addressing the limit of expert availability and alleviating the bias from overly strong assumptions about the blur and noise processes. Additionally, this research provides experimental validation of the efficacy of the newly established unified blurring and noise model, with further demonstrations of its application in single-image blind deblurring and image denoising tasks utilizing the Expectation-Maximization algorithm, with associated code publicly accessible at https://github.com/lelecheng/BlurringNoiseLimitMixtureOfExperts.

This article delves into the concept of nonassociative Yang-Baxter equations, which arise as dual solutions to specific algebraic structures. We explore the nonassociative Bogoyavlensky equation, examine its solutions in various algebraic contexts, including Lie algebras and more, and investigate its deeper mathematical implications. Additionally, we establish a key duality relationship between these equations and convolution holomorphic structures, which enables the creation of double solutions from solutioned pairs. We also establish a specific correspondence between the nonassociative Bogoyavlensky equation and the classical Yang-Baxter equation in Lie algebras, before extending the dualities to a broader 4-point framework.

Formal verification has long been a significant concern for researchers since ensuring software reliability and security demands formal validation of software specifications. The traditional approach utilizes Hoare logic, employing propositional predicates within a logical system for specification, but this is challenging for system developers to translate requirements into during validation. Recent advancements have proposed natural logic as an alternative, which mirrors informal human reasoning, and this study investigates how to apply natural logic to logical forms of system specifications. The proposed framework involves utilizing natural logic to specify software pre- and postconditions through Hoare triples, utilizing sequent calculi. Building upon this foundation, software correctness can now formally validate hoare triples, translated into natural logic, enabling logical deducibility and thus formal validation. The paper demonstrates this approach with a full program example, showing how logical forms of system specifications are formally validated, while software with propositional predicates can also be validated by translating and proving their validity within natural logic.

Consensus protocols, like Canopus, are designed to ensure various forms of failure and potential malicious attacks in distributed systems. However, existing implementations are often not resilient to real-world errors, such as node failures, network congestion, and persistent disk issues. To address this problem, Canopus+ was developed as a practical, fault-tolerant version of Canopus, capable of handling multiple types of failures. 

Canopus+ addresses implementation failures, such as timeout errors and disk persistence errors, by detecting and recovering from these specific failure types. However, Canopus+ does not protect against byzantine errors, where a node intentionally sends conflicting messages. To overcome this limitation, RCanopus, a robust Canopus implementation, was created by adding a byzantine fault detection protocol to the Canopus+ algorithm. 

Byzantine faults are classified as soft faults, where a node sends conflicting votes, or hard faults, where a node only sends a single vote despite having multiple VOTEs. Byzantine detection algorithms, such as the Oracles and Tornado, are used to identify and recover from these specific failure types. 

In experiments, RCanopus demonstrated faster recovery times compared to existing practical consensus protocols, such as Etcd, and outperformed Canbus, a byzantine-tolerant version of Canopus+ derived from CAP, despite Canbus having a shorter recovery time. Furthermore, byzantine fault detection improves the performance of RCanopus, even in benign

Our research focuses on developing and validating an efficient approach to quantify the modulus of undoped and cholesterol-infused lipid membranes through atomic force microscopy simulations. We employed the in-depth force microscopy method to map the local stiffness of lipid membranes, then integrated these findings with a probabilistic model to determine the overall flexural modulus, especially in cholesterol-infused membranes. We observed a significant increase in the flexural modulus of the DPPC membrane with rising cholesterol concentrations. To resolve a discrepancy between earlier studies, we investigated the impact of membrane doping levels and found that undoped membranes exhibit a smaller measured modulus due to uneven distribution of the undoped region. Our results demonstrate that our direct mapping technique offers a clear and accurate way to assess the local stiffness of lipid membranes and assess their mechanical properties.

We re-examine the loop quantum gravity approach to the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker spacetime, deriving it from the ADM Hamiltonian, and make modifications to obtain the quantized spacetime metric. This quantized metric leads to a differential equation that can be solved and yields a success rate of approximately 67% when compared to observed data of the cosmic expansion history, thanks to the quantum correction term's impact.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog presents an exceptional collection of ultra-high energy cosmic rays, recorded during the first operational phase between 2005 and 2022, encompassing 237 events exceeding 5.8 x 10^19 eV/s at the 90\% confidence level. Notably, this catalog includes 189 hadronic events, 28 electromagnetic ones, as well as 19 events lacking sufficient confidence for classification. Utilizing established cosmic ray models in conjunction with the catalog data, our findings suggest a discrepancy between predicted and actual hadronic ratios, indicating a significant deficit of predicted high-energy events, particularly those characterized by large shower sizes. Furthermore, this discrepancy hints at limitations in current cosmic ray models regarding the hadronic component, with implications for models assuming the strong force.

Accurately assessing uncertainty in Object Detection is a critical challenge in Deep Learning.
Although uncertainty estimation in regression tasks is more advanced, its application in Object Detection is an underexplored area of study.
Our novel Bayesian method, BayesOD, addresses this gap by incorporating Monte Carlo Dropout into existing Object Detection networks.
This approach enables uncertainty estimation for multiple model outputs by dropping out the network's dropout layers during inference.
A new uncertainty metric based on the distance between the mean and the median of sampled predictions has been devised and analyzed in relation to other metrics.
Our evaluation using the COCO dataset has provided valuable insights into the non-Gaussian nature of object detection prediction errors and highlighted the potential limitations of current uncertainty estimation methods.
Our analysis also revealed that prediction efficiency can be improved through quantile regression.
A comprehensive comparison of our approach with alternative uncertainty estimation methods has been conducted, demonstrating that object detection is a particularly difficult regression task due to its complex prediction output structure.
A thorough study of the relationship between prediction accuracy and uncertainty has been performed, revealing a suboptimal calibration in current detection models.
The findings from our analysis can guide the selection of an appropriate loss function for object detection tasks.
A comprehensive discussion on the interpretation of uncertainty in object detection has been provided.

This research paper presents novel predictions for traffic speed and volume based on short video clips of traffic conditions. While existing video-based traffic systems primarily focus on object detection and classification, our proposed method leverages these objects to create an abstract scene representation. A key innovation is the development of a hybrid hybrid model that combines Global Local Features and Convolutional Recurrent Neural Networks for determining traffic speed and volume, which outperforms recurrent and convolutional neural networks alone. Additionally, our findings reveal that video-based traffic forecasting is a relatively underexplored field and that such technologies have significant potential for practical applications.

We develop a concept of gray coherence for n-category coherence, building on the foundation of finitely presentable monads in a category with a finitely presentable monad category. Our invariance theorem demonstrates that any isomorphism between gray coherent categories preserves its structure, allowing us to establish the fact that all gray coherent categories are equivalent if they are isomorphic. Furthermore, we prove that all finite presentable n-gray categories are equivalent, assuming the condition that n equals 2.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation is crucial in neurodegenerative disease research and is used extensively by both clinicians and researchers. Deep learning techniques, particularly convolutional neural networks, have shown superiority in this application, surpassing traditional level-set methods. However, studies have shown that deep learning methods struggle with hippocampal subfields, especially in neurodegenerative conditions. To overcome this limitation, ensemble learning, a relatively unexplored approach, has been applied, where multiple hippocampus and cortex segmentation networks were trained simultaneously. These networks' output labels were then aggregated through a voting mechanism to produce a final, accurate segmentation label, significantly outperforming individual methods.

We suggest an experimental arrangement to test the phenomenon of quantum pigeonhole effect within a specific configuration of bipartite entanglement where two entangled particles are shared between two parties, Alice and Bob. This setup utilizes the properties of orbital angular momentum both for establishing nonlocal correlations and for representing quantum states that involve more than two dimensions.

The impact of trapped cosmic ray particles, specifically protons, alpha particles, and electrons, on Low Earth Orbit spacecraft has been a subject of concern. To study these effects, a simulation was conducted using Monte Carlo methods. This investigation involved modeling one-year simulations of particle trapping events at various orbital altitudes and inclinations to evaluate the probabilities of particle trap formation. From these simulations, key metrics such as the time and location of particle trap entry, as well as the relationships between elevation and other factors, were determined. Ultimately, it was found that trapped particles are more likely to be encountered by spacecraft in orbits with higher altitudes and lower inclinations.

In recent years, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been a hot topic in deep learning research, leveraging graph structures to enhance model training and performance through the integration of global and local information. However, due to the inherent limitations of current GNN designs, they often face issues related to their message-passing mechanisms, which primarily rely on uniform aggregation of neighbor node information across varying distances. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel training framework that re-wires the graph topology at an intricate level by utilizing network compression techniques. Our framework also introduces a new shrinkage skeleton structure at a macro level, incorporating a pyramid-like design with an adaptive shrinkage schedule between global coarse-grained compression steps and intricate compression steps. Our work represents a significant departure from previous research focusing on compressing network weights, as we compress the topology of the shrinkage skeleton itself, as well as the graph topology being modeled. Our experiments on complex datasets from Computer Vision and Knowledge Graph Embedding demonstrate the exceptional performance of our framework compared to state-of-the-art models.

This study introduces a novel application of the Huber loss function in matrix completion tasks performed privately. It presents and validates the effectiveness of two methodologies utilizing iterative thresholding and an iterative matrix optimization approach, both equipped with statistical privacy protections through differential privacy mechanisms. This research presents the first differential privacy achievement in matrix completion tasks performed with an arbitrary rank specification. Various numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these new methods, illustrating their superiority in privacy-preserving matrix reconstruction. Additionally, this paper provides an in-depth analysis of how data noise impacts method performance and privacy settings.

We introduce the Astrodust+PAH model, an advanced set of processes for observing interstellar dust, incorporating a detailed, microscopic-level model for how dust interacts with and emits starlight, as well as the additional influence of sub-microscopic particles in the far-infrared spectrum. The model incorporates complex interactions between particles, their charging states, and their response to starlight, as well as collisional processes and the formation of ice on particles. The model leverages existing data and advanced simulations to describe how particles behave in the interstellar medium, and includes a refined approach for observing the impact of particles on the extinction and emission of starlight, as well as their polarization. The model's development was driven by the need to create a unified framework for understanding how particles affect the extinction and emission of starlight, while also taking into account the additional influence of secondary particles in the far-infrared spectrum. The model was developed using advanced simulations and data, and its effects were carefully tested and compared to a wide range of astronomical observations, revealing a strong correlation between the model's predictions and actual astronomical data. The formation of planetary systems from initially flat protoplanetary disks is thought to involve an unknown process where planetary migration begins long before planets break up. This study examines a rare instance of a massive planet interacting with a protoplanetary disk, using ALMA observations of the star CIDA 1. Data reveal a distinct gap in the disk, accompanied by asymmetrical rings, indicating interactions between a planet and dust grains. A particular feature in the disk, likely a plume of material swept up by a pressure front moving across its outer edge, is consistent with theoretical models of planet-disk interactions. Data indicate that a planet of at least 0.3 Jupiter masses, located between 10-14 astronomical units away, is responsible for a gap of around 5 astronomical units in radius. The study finds that the disk's outer rings, located at about 22-24 astronomical units, could be explained by the accumulation of material following a gap, and also due to the interaction of a planet's gravitational effects with the behavior of small particles. The study concludes that the formation of planets like Jupiter likely began through a process of disk instability, and early planetary migration, driven by interactions with the disk, is a common occurrence.

We investigate an extension of the Lights Out game, referred to as the Most Taps version, where we aim to achieve a state where every button is turned off after the minimum number of actions. This state corresponds to when the total number of times a button is pressed is odd, or in matrix terms, the button state vector $b$ satisfies the condition $A \cdot b = 0 \pmod 2$. This vector $b$ represents the accumulated button state after the minimum number of taps. We develop solutions for matrix $A$ with entries $a_{i,j} = 1$ if $|i-j| \leq k$ and $0$ otherwise, for a non-negative integer $k$, using recursive formulas for determinant and permanent of matrix $A$. These solutions yield a matrix $b$ that is also tridiagonal with $b_{i,j} = 1$ if $k+1 \mid |i-j|$.

This research proposes an image segmentation model, inspired by variational image segmentation models, that incorporates image restoration techniques such as deblurring, de-noising, and de-hazing. The paper addresses the challenges associated with the traditional model's performance, which can be hindered by ill-posedness and rayleigh-like instability, leading to subpar image segmentation and image image effects during image differentiators evolution. To overcome these limitations, a multi-stage optimization strategy, combining global and local searches, is presented to optimize image differentiators within the energy functional. Additionally, this method utilizes second-order information, represented by hessian matrices, to enhance convergence efficiency. The algorithm is evaluated through various synthetic experiments, demonstrating its ability to effectively segment images and accurately estimate image differentiators while overcoming the aforementioned limitations.

To enhance the performance of Abstract Interpretation, especially for programs with recursive or high-performance demands, a strategy involves decoupling the rising and descending parts of these programs during the analysis. By separating these parts, rising phase analysis can be optimized using previously developed techniques, such as vector space completion, to determine a constraint that limits resource consumption to within a specified bound. However, the analysis of the descending phase, involving unrolling constraints, can be a time-consuming and bottlenecking task, especially when unrolling is done to a high count. To mitigate this constraint, a new approach has been introduced in this study, which focuses on the construction of a control flow graph, which is then used to guide a costly but effective fixed-point analysis, which in turn enables a much simpler fixed-point calculation and enables a much smaller number of unrollings, which in turn enables the significant speedup of the analysis.

Researchers have been inspired by the discovery of topological phonons in mechanical systems and quantum crystals, driving them to explore non-oxide perovskites.  In this research, we investigate how manipulating oxide perovskites with an open-shell transition metal influences their topological phonon properties.  Using first-principles calculations and a simple model, we found that altering the oxidation state and electronic configuration allows us to control topological phonons through two mechanisms: adjusting the size of the oscillating oscillator and manipulating the system's symmetry.  This discovery reveals that we can achieve a diverse range of topological phonon characteristics in oxide perovskites, potentially leading to the development of new functional materials in the near future.

Unsupervised classification of outliers in diverse datasets is a widely recognized challenge addressed by numerous established methods. However, many conventional outlier detection algorithms are limited to working with dataset points with specific numerical attributes and rely on pre-defined calculations to measure distances. This study introduces a novel outlier detection method applicable to datasets of any dimensionality, using an outlier network constructed from the data's inherent distances. This framework accommodates various proximity graph constructions, including nearest neighbor networks, measure maintenance and update techniques for efficient and accurate outlier detection. Notably, even the fastest variant of the approach achieves a remarkable 1000 times speedup compared to prior arts with equivalent accuracy.

The motion of a mirror causes it to displace electronic clouds within atoms, and this displacement can be measured as a measure of atomic displacement.
This phenomenon, and others related to it, can be utilized for developing novel atomic displacement sensors.
The coefficients governing electric dipole (ED) and electric quadrupole (EQ) contributions to atomic displacement have been derived for both hydrogen and alkali atoms.
Two additional phenomena related to atomic displacement have been found. Firstly, changes in ED and EQ distribution can produce a permanent electric dipole moment due to their asymmetry, and this property can be exploited to create highly sensitive electric field sensors.
The magnitude of these changes, known as electric displacement induced polarization (EDIP) and electric quadrupole displacement (EQD), can be quantified by corresponding coefficients.
A second phenomenon, motion-induced stimulation of higher-order electric multipoles within an atom due to its quadrupole component, was also observed.
This phenomenon, known as electric quadrupole displacement induced polarization (EQDIP), was found to be weaker than the EDIP, but its magnitude can be enhanced by adjusting the quadrupole component of the mirror's field.
The atoms' displacement also leads to a modified electric quadrupole moment, and this change, known as electric quadrupole displacement (EQD), was found to produce electric quadrupole radiation (EQR) with its unique characteristics.

When training a graph-based predictive model, the outcomes can vary greatly due to fairness concerns. To mitigate this, we have developed a framework for enforcing fairness in graph settings. Our approach ensures that the predictive model's results remain consistent across different groups of connected nodes, especially when the groups are located on the graph periphery. By transforming the fairness issue into an optimization problem, we can effectively apply our method to real-world graph data, such as the Facebook friendship network. Notably, our approach is highly effective with limited data available from the groups, resulting in predictive models that not only adhere to fairness standards but also maintain accuracy.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme processes, where traditional methods for generating approximate solutions from equilibrium states often fail due to nonconvergent iterations. In contrast, new solutions consistently reach convergence and are derived using a systematic approach. These approximate solutions can be adjusted for greater accuracy by using exact equilibrium constants and exact rate constants calculated through perturbation theory. These findings apply to various enzyme processes, under a broad range of kinetic mechanisms.

Based on a 139 fb$^{-1}$ dataset collected at 13 TeV from proton-proton collisions, researchers have explored a broad array of supersymmetry models that involve the direct production of pair of simplified models consisting of either top quarks and dark matter or gluinos and dark matter, paired with one or more soft particles such as a bottom quark, a bottomron, a light scalar or charged Higgs boson, or a neutralino. These studies examined scenarios where the gluino or top quark masses were as low as 200 GeV. Research results have shown no evidence of new physics, leading to 95% confidence level upper limits on various supersymmetry model scenarios. Notably, for models involving the direct production of top quarks and dark particles accompanied by a bottom quark, researchers have established upper limits as low as 1.1 TeV for models involving a heavy scalar and charged Higgs. These limits are in line with current bounds on models involving a large number of light scalars in divided models and divided models containing a light scalar and three light neutralinos. These divided models containing a light scalar and three light neutralinos are found to have upper limits as low as 1.1 TeV as well.
