Existing tools for interactive visualization are vast, but adapting them specifically to these data types requires further investigation and targeted development.

A prominent feature in various applications of the modern neural network model, graph neural networks (GNNs), excels in learning node and graph-level representations by capturing the structural and attribute-based similarities within a graph. To date, most GRL methods focus on flat (i.e., pairwise) resemblance, which is often insufficient for complex data such as sequential and hierarchical patterns. We introduce the Heterogeneous resemblance graph neural network (HRGNN), which builds upon GRL via custom graph neural networks (GNNs) to learn more expressive node and graph-level representations that can be applied to the analysis of electronic health records (EHRs). We demonstrate the efficacy of HRGNN on three key tasks: (i) learning representational embeddings of diseases, (ii) diagnosing diseases based on EHRs, and (iii) predicting a patient's outcome. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on three public datasets (MIMIC, MIMIC-Japan, and MIMIC-UHC-KSTAR) by showing the superiority of HRGNN over leading baselines such as HDBOC, the U-Net, and the fully connected neural network.

This study explores the impact of electrostatic interactions within the electric double layer on the properties of soft polymers with permanent charge using molecular dynamics simulations. We employ two distinct solvent models: a coarse-grained model treating the solvent as structureless and an atomistic model considering individual solvent molecules. We compare these models with each other and with results from continuum theory. A solvent polarisation effect significantly affects the electric double layer structure when the surface charge is high, resulting in noticeable structural changes due to the arrangement of counterions. In contrast, for surfaces with lower charges, the models exhibit little to no difference. Additionally, we investigate how local dielectric changes affect the polymer chain conformations. A strong electrostatic interaction within the electric double layer significantly affects the polymer conformations due to the solvent polarisation effect and local dielectric changes.

This study demonstrates that well-trained BERT models can effectively extract software elements from textual sources. We developed two distinct transformer-based architectures that recognize software features based on pre-defined categories and free-text inputs, respectively. Experimental results show high accuracy in extracting software requirements and code, achieving 94.2% and 96.1% respective precision and recall rates for the first architecture, and 89.2% precision and 75.3% recall rates for the second architecture's broader software element classification. Notably, our model's capacity to identify the semantic significance of terms like "code" or "requirements" contributes to its high F1 score in the second architecture's stricter binary classification scenario.

A one-way communication network with multiple relays is analyzed and enhanced through collaborative network coding, a process that allows relays to exchange data efficiently by computing the XOR operation on received signals, thus reducing encoding-decoding complexity. We've developed an innovative method, a energy-efficient XOR selection algorithm, to minimize the energy consumption for relay collaboration. Additionally, a joint scheduling and power allocation scheme has been devised to tackle the difficulty in modern networks where there's a need to balance encoding efficiency and user experience through fair and adaptable data transmission. Our proposed approach, a two-stage algorithm, initially aims to minimize energy consumption through joint scheduling of relays and power allocation at source and relay stations. In the second stage, we've tackled the problem of achieving a balance between minimum energy consumption and user quality of experience through energy-efficient power allocation and scheduling of relays. Our numerical results confirm that the proposed techniques significantly reduce energy consumption and improve system performance.

A first-principles theory, incorporating relativistic effects and implemented using Dirac-Kohn-Sham methods, has been developed to study Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states in more complex materials.  An application of this theory involves the study of an Mn adatom and Mn clusters on Nb(110), where it is found that a key characteristic of these systems, their zero-temperature energy gap, can be accurately predicted using this approach.  Furthermore, variations in the system's symmetry, size, and composition are found to significantly impact the system's properties and lead to significant systematic behavior in the system's energy gap.  A significant advantage of this approach is that it does not require any user input or adjustments, making it a reliable and accurate method for predicting and understanding Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states in more complex and intricate Yu--Shiba--Rusinov state host materials.

The FASER$\mathrm{K}$ experiment, a new particle search, aimed to investigate the $K^+$ meson's decay into a $\pi^+$ and invisible particles at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021. Utilizing a 12-meter-long, 900-meter-downstream special detector located at the LHC's interaction point, researchers observed a 12.6-GeV $K^+$ meson sample. Analyzing this data, a 90% confidence interval exclusion limit was found, which is the first instance at high energy. It also sets an extremely precise branching fraction upper bound at 3.02$\times$10$^{-4}$, with a corresponding 2.0$\times$10$^{-4}$ statistical value. Compared to theoretical predictions based on the Standard Model, a discrepancy was found, prompting a call for more sensitive experiments and improved measurements.

This study introduces a method to mitigate the effects of rotationally asymmetric environments on 3D LiDAR scan matching. The proposed approach is built upon 2D image-based distribution matching and utilizes a one-layer CNN to create rotation-invariant image features. The resulting features, when compared, yield an orientation that is unaffected by the angle at which the scans are rotated. The application of this method to LiDAR data leads to improved and more reliable match results, particularly in environments that are sensitive to orientation. The features generated by the model, known as LF-CNN, exhibit strong properties for image matching, and their use significantly enhances the accuracy of LiDAR orientation estimation, with a notable reduction in error rates, up to 20 degrees, when compared to traditional methods, when the actual orientation error exceeds a certain threshold.

Deep networks demonstrate superior performance in computer vision tasks but several factors still require further research, particularly the reliance on vast datasets and limited understanding of decision-making processes. To overcome these challenges, particularly the dependency on large datasets, we propose an innovative approach to satellite-based edge detection, enabling the utilization of network distillation and particularly leveraging transfer learning in unsupervised settings. This leads to notable advancements in the utilization of network distillation, as we demonstrate that our approach yields better results than supervised methods on large satellite datasets like Places2. Furthermore, we successfully apply our technique to a network smaller than the commonly used ResNet50, achieving nearly identical outcomes while significantly reducing the training requirements, encompassing diverse textures in satellite images to enhance the transferability of the training process.

High-energy, intense X-ray pulses enable the capture of detailed spectral fluctuations over a broad energy range. This process captures dynamic changes in core electrons and reveals the behavior of valence electrons, an approach beneficial for studying complex materials and the development of ultrafast techniques. Utilizing advanced simulation software, researchers can enhance the accuracy of these measurements by shifting from a single-electron model to a multi-electron model. In this study, we present a rate model that accounts for the ionization of multiple electron groups and correlates with experimental data across three case studies: the absorption of a krypton target and the changes in the L3 absorption edge of lanthanum sesquioxide, La$_{2}$O$_{3}$. By considering the simultaneous ionization of several electron groups, the model captures the complexity of non-linear XANES spectra.

This paper examines the vulnerability of Classification via Deep Learning (CLDD) systems for Digital Modulation Classification, targeting the generation of diverse, realistic samples under various attacks to create a more robust classifier. A novel Deep Generative Adversarial Network (DGDA) is presented to create deep fakes under multiple attacks, and the proposed Binary Discriminative Neural Network (BDNN) is designed to classify both original and DGDA-generated data under various attacks, exhibiting superior performance against classification. Theoretical justifications for DGDA and BDNN are provided, and the proposed methods are demonstrated to be more effective than Differential Privacy (DP) and a comparison classifier.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is a complex task due to the
potential pitfalls of reusing public datasets, as they may not always reflect
current conditions. A specific example is the MS lesion challenge hosted on
ISBI in 2020, where the goal was to develop an accurate lesion mask
segmentation model. In our study, we compare the performance of two
approaches: a continuous learning model, and a from scratch model, and evaluate
their effectiveness compared to a third method, ensemble learning. By applying
these techniques to datasets from different hospitals, we demonstrate the
efficacy of continuous learning as a low-resource alternative to ensemble
learning, offering a robust and scalable solution for this medical imaging
challenge.

A novel technique for achieving bipolar contrast in quantum 2D imaging is introduced and implemented using a double potential well system. By preparing a two-component 2D gas in a specific quantum state, we can create a reference wavefunction that interferes with the target wavefunction, resulting in a bipartite image with enhanced contrast. Compared to the conventional single-well imaging method, the bipolar contrast technique doubles the contrast while reducing the required spatial resolution, thus improving the overall imaging quality. Notably, the bipolar contrast is resilient to variations in the probe's initial phase, broadening the applicability of the method in the quantum regime where phase stability is often compromised. Furthermore, the proposed bipolar contrast image exhibits a binary pattern, which holds significant value for applications in quantum computing, where it can be employed for measurements of quantum entanglement and other related phenomena.

Statistical learning techniques allow us to create a function that quantifies the discrepancy between accurate simulations from complex models and less computationally demanding approximations. This holds relevance not just for simplified models but also for reducing the cost of simulations using approximated models when running high-resolution simulations would be too computationally expensive. We develop a theoretical framework for a data-driven approach that learns the error in a less computationally intensive approximation and uses this information to improve upon it. This enhanced strategy leads to more accurate results and offers theoretical guarantees that the improved model will outperform the initial approximation for a given task. We test our approach on a modified model based on the 2D Navier-Stokes equations and find it effective at addressing this issue.

A detailed 70-micron map of the Dragon Infared Dark Cloud (IRDC), centered on L1449, reveals a core expansion phenomenon occurring just outside its photosphere. This core expansion is particularly noticeable, reaching its maximum at the core's edge. An outflow from the core has also been detected. The core expansion and outflow can't be fully explained by thermal properties or dust sublimation. A simplified model suggests the core expansion is a result of the core's internal heat generation pushing against its surroundings. This implies the core's internal heat is a sign of recent, massive star birth.

Theoretical primordial black holes (PBHs) formed in the early universe provide a conceivable origin for dark matter. Although PBHs are likely not linked to our current understanding of dark matter, they remain an intriguing possibility, and their mass lifespan is not significantly influenced by Hawking radiation. Consequently, a detailed investigation of PBH mass formation is crucial, particularly if some of these black holes eventually contribute to dark matter. To approach this issue, we've employed the PopSyCLE framework, which enables us to examine PBH mass distributions and formative scenarios under various dark matter conditions. Our analysis reveals that PBH formation and their mass can be influenced by factors such as spatial fragmentation and magnetic field patterns.

Building on a previous study that examined equilibrium states of particles of varying sizes, this paper explores configurations where the arrangement varies across space. Through our simulations, particles of uniform sizes but differing lengths were discovered to have stable varying wedge orientations known as the N_splay phase at intermediate densities, and a N_2-splay phase at higher densities. As interaction strength decreases, these structures transition into modulations known as splay-1 and splay-2. Interestingly, S splay phases at low densities are bounded by the Isometric fluid phase and the N_splay phase, while S is itself enclosed by the N_splay and fluid (F) phases, which are both in turn bounded by the N_splay and hexagonal crystal phases. Our research reveals multiple transitions between these states, including S to N, S to F, N to hexagonal crystal, and F to hexagonal crystal, with some being continuous and others being first-order. Furthermore, this paper investigates the stability of the N_splay phase, revealing its various boundaries.

Recent advancements in the field of machine learning have seen a significant surge in model sizes and the development of the Adapter architecture, a form of Pareto-efficient parameter optimization for fine-tuning large models. Adapters, designed to modify a base model's output, use task-agnostic intermediate tokens to represent a fine-tuning task and then modify the base model's final tokens. However, we argue that intermediate tokens may not be the optimal indicator of a fine-tuning task's characteristics. Therefore, we propose a novel approach that utilizes a task-specific last-layer embedding, known as the Special Token Adaptation architecture, to retrain the intermediate and final tokens. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach is more effective than the existing adapter methods, and we provide theoretical justification for its efficacy.

This paper revisits a class of algorithmic issues involving the assignment of linear preferences to elements within a set and its subsets to optimize their combined value. The research focuses on the role of contextual preferences, which can change when an element is added to a subset, contrasting with global preferences, which remain unchanged. The study demonstrates the computational complexities of the two approaches, highlighting the advantage of global preferences, which can be computed in linear time. The researchers also present efficient polynomial-time algorithms for the contextual preferences when they depend on only a limited number of variables. The critical question of whether the contextual preferences can be approximately approximated with global preferences is answered in the affirmative with an approximation ratio of $\sqrt{n/2}$. The final section of the paper explores hardness and approximation issues when the contextual preferences depend on only a single variable.

Recent scientific research has identified macroscopic thermodynamic dynamics as a key factor in controlling the glass transition. Following up on this discovery, we conducted a comprehensive assessment of various thermodynamic metrics for several polymer fluids near the glass transition point. Our investigation involved analyzing liquid volumes, entropies, enthalpies, and the activity coefficients of a wide range of polymers with different cooling rates. Notably, we observed that certain measures of thermodynamic nonequilibrium, calculated using a different theoretical framework, are closely correlated with materials' relaxation times. Moreover, these metrics can even predict the changes in relaxation times. These recent findings reinforce the idea that simple thermodynamic dynamics can serve as proxy indicators for the complex time-dependent behavior of glass-forming fluids.

Fine-tuning large pre-trained language models for tasks typically involves using masked sequence prediction. However, this method has been associated with a phenomenon known as the "decontextualization effect," where the model's developmentally acquired knowledge is lost due to the task's demand for rejecting information. To Decontextualization Effect. To better understand this issue, we created a new benchmark called REJECT, consisting of five tasks that require both making statements and rejecting embedded information from a context. Our analysis shows.

Our study proposes a new approach, known as Look-ahead Focus for Generation (LFG), in neural machine translation. The LFG mechanism utilizes future target context to guide the translation process, enhancing context-sensitive decoding without increasing model complexity. To achieve this, we employ future target words from the training data and an additional decoder layer that shares parameters with the main translation model. Our results on a variety of NMT datasets demonstrate that LFG significantly improves generation qualities, validating its potential for more robust and adaptable NL systems.

This study calculates the Kontsevich weights of curvature and connection graphs within the framework of symplectic PO_n^WO holomorphic deformations. Our capacity to compute these weights enables us to derive the formula for the Kontsevich weight of a generic Kontsevich graph, marking a pivotal advancement over previous methods constrained to specific forms. Furthermore, this result facilitates a formulation in PO_n^WO context of a novel connection and curvature pair satisfying the flatness condition, thus symbolically representing a symplectic PO_n^WO analogue of the Drinfeld double of a Lie algebra.

This study focuses on open regions of $d$-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs), examining the dynamics and equilibrium states. Our analysis involves deformations, specifically relevant and irrelevant operators, of large central charge CFTs in $d$ dimensions. Initially, we investigate the entanglement entropy of a spherical entanglement entropy and correlation functions in the thermal state for irrelevant operator deformations. Notably, we apply the bootstrap method, which enables us to establish an inequality among relevant parameters, leading to the conclusion that the entanglement entropy of a spherical entanglement in the thermal state exhibits increased positivity for specific deformation scenarios. Additionally, we conduct an in-depth study on the entanglement entropy of a spherical entanglement in deformed CFTs, specifically for the case of Lagrangian subtheories. Our results, derived using large $N$ expansion, demonstrate that the entanglement entropy demonstrates effective relevant-irrelevant mixing. Ultimately, we draw a comparison with a causal diamond in deformed $2+1$ dimensions, and contrast thermal and entanglement properties.

Zhang's 2010 paper introduced a universal pricing method for Asian options using a potential function, though a key equation for calculating this potential was incorrectly written. Our paper corrects this mistake by presenting a new, accurate potential function and associated calculation. We also apply this improvement to develop exact pricing methods for Asian options with various underlying Markov processes, including those with finite or continuous states.

The discovery of dispersed gamma rays emitted by clusters of galaxies, which could be observed by future gamma-ray telescellites, is based on the idea that new galactic formations contribute to this emission. Specifically, the EAGLE simulation predicted a dispersed gamma ray signal from clusters, measured at energies of 10 TeV. Observations from the Fermi LAT at 300 GeV show that the current limits on dispersed gamma rays are consistent with emission from clusters, which could be observed by next-generation telescellites.

The foundational "hot big bang" model of cosmology is supplemented by additional mechanisms, such as cosmological collider physics, which can produce post-inflationary signals imprinted on the primordial universe. Researchers investigate a new model where a massive particle decays during inflation, resulting in correlations in the primordial universe's power spectrum. While the standard "consistency check" for cosmological collider physics assumes an unperturbed ("prismatic") feature spectrum, this work explores how "smearing" effects from noise and instrumental limitations impact these signals. They employ machine learning techniques to assess the resilience of these signals, and their results suggest that these post-inflationary signals can be reliably detected by future experiments, even when their spectra are significantly smoothed.

Despite their impressive performance, deep convolutional neural networks remain opaque. To gain insight into their internal workings, we've developed a method to clear up confusion within these networks by concentrating on specific features within their latent visual representations, linking them to the activation of relevant semantic categories through class maps. By comparing the effectiveness of various ways to concentrate on these features, including minimum filtering, we found that it helps to simplify the visual representations, revealing more definitive patterns and a more structured hierarchy within the network. Moreover, this approach sheds light on the nature of bias in feature attention, particularly among disparate images, and illustrates its connection to early pattern matching. Ultimately, this approach enhances the interpretability of deep convolutional neural networks, contributing to more trustworthy AI systems.

A recent decision theory study on one-dimensional cuprates suggests an attractive bond between neighboring copper sites, leading to the assumption of a specific electron order. By utilizing density functional calculations, we discovered that this specific electron order can be validated by considering both electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions. Our calculations demonstrate that this order causes significant shifts in certain energy bands and modifies the density of states within certain copper sites, which can be observed in experiments and implies a metal-insulator transition triggered by this order. The proposed mechanism involving phonines provides an explanation for the superconducting properties in one-dimensional cuprates, despite initial doubts about their existence at low temperatures.

A novel causal inference framework, Causal Structure Learning from Time Series Data (CSL-TD), is developed for learning causal structures from time series data. This is achieved through time embedding of data, maximization of an information metric, and time-based structure analysis. An existing method, Causal Structural Discovery-Time Series Data Analysis (CSD-TDA), is adapted and evaluated using synthesized time series data. Building upon this work, CSD-TDA is applied to analyze structures within Malawi's Immunization, Health, Maternal and Child Survival Program (MPHIA) dataset. This study further demonstrates the impact of time lags and data pre-processing on causal structure learning and presents a detailed causal model of child growth and nutritional status based on the inferred structure and parametric estimates.

The presence of unstable skyrmion lattices, characterized by their quick decay, 
has not been extensively examined in experimental settings. Studies on $Cu_2$Mn$_2$Ge, 
where these lattices spontaneously emerge, lack control over their formation 
conditions. Our research involves applying an external magnetic field to manipulate 
the stability of skyrmion phases in Mn-based alloys, including $Co_9$Zn$9$Mn$_2$, 
enabling a more in-depth examination. Our observations demonstrate a precise 
correlation between the coexistence of two distinct magnetic phases and the rapid 
decay of skyrmions, as revealed by small-angle neutron scattering. Our findings 
indicate that this decay is due to the disruption of the skyrmion pattern by another 
magnetic phase, rather than thermal fluctuations. Moreover, our research 
indicates that the rapid decay of skyrmions is not the sole outcome of their 
instability. Instead, an optimal balance between energy instability and dynamic 
stability is required for these skyrmions to persist over time.

Linear observation models, often used for forecasting due to their simplicity and interpretability, face limitations in handling large datasets with many variables. To address this issue, state-space modeling has been enhanced through the development of variable models, although this area is still in its early stages. A significant portion of the current literature focuses on static variable models, leaving dynamic variable models underresearched. This paper aims to provide an overview of high-dimensional dynamic variable models to facilitate understanding and identify potential future research paths.

This paper introduces a novel optimization problem and demonstrates its connection to both the Banach fixed point theorem and the Hamilton-Jacobi equation. By applying the Cosine of Bregman Proximal Hamilton-Jacobi-Viscous equation, we derive an approximate solution using a computable formula. Furthermore, we investigate the numerical solution's stability and provide a proof of its convergence.

Recent advancements in reversible information hiding have shown significant potential for practical applications, primarily focusing on color images. This research aims to address the limitations of current methods by introducing a new technique using Bayesian neural networks. This novel approach allows for the efficient extraction of hidden data from various image types in a single step, and when applied to color images, it successfully retrieves the original data without affecting the chroma components.

The primary goal of this research was to understand how various types of turbulent effects impact mean-field dynamos. Specifically, it focused on two types: turbulent diffusion and Hall terms. By applying these to mean-field models, it's been discovered that dynamos can arise in regions where turbulent magnetic field is aligned with background flow. However, in these same regions, the magnetic field is amplified in a similar orientation to alpha-effect. Our findings suggest that the required scale separation for the alpha-dynamo is narrower than previously thought. Nonetheless, the inclusion of odd-order turbulent effects, such as Hall terms, led to the emergence of a new type of dynamo with an opposite magnetic field orientation. In contrast to even-order turbulent effects, the odd-order dynamo doesn't produce magnetic field in the same direction as the alpha-effect. Our research indicates that the combined action of even and odd-order turbulent effects results in a helical dynamo, which is similar to the alpha-dynamo but more resilient. The effect of magnetic field on turbulent viscosity and viscosity of helicity appears minimal, but the effect of magnetic field on helicity viscosity derived from turbulent closure is significant. The application of this research to stars reveals that the alpha-dynamo and helical dynammo are likely to operate in stars with radiative cores, while regions without magnetic field may still generate dynamos due to convection arising from buoyancy.

The galaxy, NGC4945, exhibits significant star formation activity and hosts an active galactic nucleus of type Seyfert 2. Our observations using the ALMA telescope, specifically the $^{12}$CO J=1-0 emission lines in the nuclear area, reveal the presence of a molecular cloud complex highly energized by the AGN's outflow. The data indicate that the emission is not a uniform disk, but rather a cloud complex. The emission line's morphology is elongated, oriented at 70 degrees to the galaxy's major axis. The mass of the observed molecular gas is approximately 1.5 million solar masses. The molecular gas velocity difference between the outflowing and galaxy rotation velocities is about 175 km/s. The molecular gas density in the ejecta is estimated to be 100-1000 times the density in the solar neighborhood. The effect of the AGN's outflow on the molecular cloud complex results in an observed bolometric luminosity of approximately $10^8$ times the luminosity of the sun. The data suggest that a supermassive black hole is expelling molecular gas at a rate of about $10^3$ times the mass of the sun per year, with the specific mechanism behind the AGN's outflow still to be determined.

A novel, high-performance method has been developed to numerically solve complex equations describing magnetized plasma behaviors, particularly in fusion and astrophysical contexts, where multiple scales and interfaces pose significant challenges. Placing key conservation properties at the core of its algorithm ensures that the algorithm maintains accuracy and reliability. A specific approach uses high-order polynomial functions within an unstructured mesh framework to accurately capture details of current density and its surrounding magnetic fields. Notably, even with lower-order schemes, this method achieves high-order accuracy in simulating magnetic field lines. To expedite convergence, a specific technique incorporates an unconventional numerical magnetic flux into its unstructured mesh. A comprehensive comparison demonstrates the algorithm's superior performance in plasma modeling using a specific example of turbulent plasma formed by magnetic field interactions in a tokamak.

This study introduces a new differential equation modulated SDIMSIM, parameterized by a positive constant α, which enables adaptation to general standard ordinary differential equations through the incorporation of a positive stepsize parameter τ, also conditioned by α. The proposed SDIMSIM's stability properties are analyzed and evaluated and it is demonstrated that, for an optimal choice of α and τ, even the backward differentiation formulas of order one to four exhibit algebraic stability, enabling convergence of semi-discrete and fully-discrete solutions to parabolic problems and convergence of fully-discrete solutions to hyperbolic problems. Furthermore, this method is capable of achieving high spatial and temporal convergence for wave equations. The method's efficiency is highlighted and compared to a variable stepsize geometric SDIMSIM previously proposed in the literature.

We develop a theory of exponential stability for semigroups generated by linear C0-semigroups on Banach spaces through a variation of the Lyapunov operator equation, adapting it from its well-established counterpart in finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. This approach provides a novel resolution to a long-standing open problem in the field of operator theory.

To aid muon-based CPT-symmetry testing, the MuMuPy python calculator was created. It simulates the dimuon pair decay from muon muon collision and subsequent muon-scattering interaction with various materials placed in the inlaid position of the experimental setup. By integrating Rayleigh scattering cross-sections with物质的 density and molecular composition, MuMuPy estimates energy loss, energy loss rate, and the track lengths of muons as they traverse the chosen material. By allowing users to input the energy of individual muons, the MuMuPy calculator can be tailored to specific scenarios in which dimuon decay is applied, resulting in considerable performance optimization.

portfolio theory has seen a significant resurgence in recent years due to widespread adoption of the $L_p$-risk measure for asset allocation under uncertainty. Specifically, the $L_2$-risk measure led to efficient portfolio selection methods utilizing quadratic models and fast numerical algorithms. In contrast, the $L_1$-risk measure offered valuable properties such as robustness against asset returns fluctuations, making it suitable for time series analysis in the short term. This research investigates robust portfolio models grounded in a power utility of a general $L_p$-risk ($p \neq 1$) measure, considering both absolute and relative assets. It examines the efficient frontier and stochastic dominance properties for various $p$ values and reveals a key finding: while stochastically dominating other portfolios, the robust frontier does not always surpass non-risk-robust frontiers. This study also establishes numerical connections between the robust and non-robust frameworks.

The cosmic evolution of dwarf galaxies is intricately tied to the surrounding intergalactic and interstellar mediums, whose properties and histories are still largely unknown. To effectively model and understand the transformation of galaxies, researchers must establish precise descriptions of the gas and metals present in these mediums. We suggest adopting a comprehensive approach centered on observation, enabling scientists to accurately reconstruct the evolution of the intergalactic medium and predict the future growth of galaxies through self-consistent modeling. This review focuses on the current understanding of dwarf galaxies and their environs, with an emphasis on the role of interstellar and intergalactic mediums in shaping galaxy evolution. We explore existing observational findings, discuss future prospects, and outline critical challenges in this field.

A key element in understanding the low-energy behavior of ultracold atoms in optical lattices and other similar systems involves the Anderson model, particularly in the context of localized fermions interacting with delocalized ones and a correlated bosonic environment. In this analysis, we investigate a system consisting of one-dimensional, partially filled lattices where a single-site fermionic lattice experiences weak disorder and interacts strongly with a single-dimensional phonon field modeled after the Holstein model via a local Hubbard-Stratonovich field. We uncover a novel collapse phenomenon where fermionic quasiparticles disappear, even in the absence of fermionic quasiparticle instability. Upon a phase transition triggered by phonon-mediated interactions between the two lattices, we observe a length-scale divergence associated with the fermionic quasiparticles, characterized by either a phonon-driven gap opening or the emergence of non-local fermionic constraints resulting in an incompressible lattice. The observed length-scale divergence shares similarities with a prior study revealing a correlation between quasiparticle collapse and the lattice's charge ordering properties.

The divergence of a group is a measure of how efficiently its elements can be expressed as products of generators, with its asymptotic behavior illustrated by a divergence function. A group is considered highly complex when its divergence grows at a polynomial rate, and we have further categorised such groups based on specific growth rate properties. We've determined the divergence characteristics of an extensive range of Thompson's and Braided Thompson's group variants, with significant implications for understanding theThompson groups' overall behaviour.

This article examines the Question-Answering task with a focus on utilizing 
the Retrieval-Augmented-Generation framework with a DPR retriever, as well as 
evaluating various approaches to pre-training the DPR model, including fine-tuning 
the model both before and after training, using a combination of exact matching 
and F1 metrics for the evaluation of generated answers.

The author modifies and ultimately generalizes a previous polynomial system for which he was unable to derive an explicit inner product, and observes that the derived asymptotics closely resemble those of Jacobi polynomials. This result is based on the employing the渊method of reproducing kernels in the relevant space.

We investigated the difficulties Amazon Mechanical Turk workers face in locating top-tier individuals for studies on Plato's Cave, a concept requiring knowledge of both philosophy and art. We discovered that a significant number of participants failed to provide a suitable response due to unwarranted rejections, which posed several challenges. Firstly, we struggled to identify qualified workers, even in straightforward tasks. Secondly, we struggled to convince less-experienced workers to submit responses despite their rejections. Thirdly, we found it difficult to recruit experienced workers despite their high approval rates. We suggest that MTurk researchers should reassess their reliance on qualified workers and consider new strategies to avoid relying on flawed datasets.

The challenge of text-video representation learning lies in aligning the temporal aspects of visual and auditory information. Current top-tier video indexing systems rely on a combination of pre-trained image and audio feature extractors, and a few fully trainable modules. However, these pre-trained models lack the ability to capture the semantic nuances of videos and their captions. Recent research has explored the use of a Transformer-based architecture for text-video representation learning, but these approaches fail to leverage the information from both individual details and the overall context of the video data. In this research, we introduce TS2-Net, a novel approach that combines the strengths of a Transformer architecture with the capabilities of a mechanism for selecting and shifting the most relevant visual and auditory information. By incorporating this mechanism, TS2-Net can effectively focus on key regions and their relationships, while also adapting the pre-existing feature models. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that TS2-Net achieves remarkable performance in the MTEC video dataset, as well as in the FAIR dataset, with results that consistently surpass the current state-of-the-art methods.

A new flavor-changing neutral top quark neutral current $u+d+\gamma$ has been identified within a particular $E_6$ gauge symmetry model, specifically in a scenario involving a symmetry breakdown pattern of $SU(5)\times U(1)_\chi \times S_3 \rightarrow SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$. This process poses significant challenges to the $t\rightarrow c+\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow u+\gamma$ transitions following a top quark flavor oscillation, with both transitions being time-dependent and neutral radiative transitions gaining prominence over non-radiative transitions under certain conditions. A novel time-dependent ratio $R_\gamma$ can be utilized to experimentally verify the occurrence of flavor oscillations and gauge boson $Z'$ mediation effects at a given energy scale, with $S_3$ flavor oscillations being inherently $CP$ even despite potential $CP$ odd effects from $V_{CHQ}$ and $V_{UQ}$. Furthermore, a novel ratio $R_\Lambda$ can be employed to experimentally confirm the presence of flavor oscillations at the same energy scale by measuring the ratio of cross-sections of weak transitions $t\rightarrow c+q\bar{q}$ and $t\rightarrow u+q\bar{q}$. Additionally, a new ratio $R_Z$ is proposed to experimentally verify $Z'$ coupling to $q+

In our analysis, a generalized network model is studied, combining preferred attachment and an equal probability connection rule. This altered network evolves over time by introducing a new node, which forms multiple directed connections. Each possible connection is preferred based on an individual's preferred attachment rules, yet unestablished rules are given equal probability. Our findings confirm that the degree distribution of highly connected nodes follows a power law, while our equal probability connection rule gave rise to a normal distribution of highly connected nodes' degrees.

A Convolutional Neural Network model is introduced to detect and track wireless signal interference on a smartphone and to predict the interference level. To collect data, a study using 100 participants on the Shanghai Metro Line 13 smartphone survey app detected signal interference on the go. Results showed a high correlation between the detector and tracker modules, confirming the consistency of outcomes. Results also demonstrated that a Convolutional Neural Network model is effective in identifying and tracking wireless signal interference on a mobile device, showcasing its level of accuracy and other performance metrics. To collect training data, the GRU neural network model is utilized to label images captured by the detector, and the GRU neural network is trained to label wireless signal interference on the detector. To collect training data for the tracker module, matrix images are generated from binary maps of interference data, and the tracker module is trained to predict interference data on the go. To detect signal interference on a mobile device, a detector module is used to collect data on the device, and a tracker module is used to process the data and predict interference data on the device. To train the model, 100 participants on the go detected signal interference on the Shanghai Metro Line 13 smartphone app, and the results showed that the model achieved high accuracy on the go. To evaluate the model, accuracy, recall, and other performance metrics are calculated on the go, and the results showed that the model achieved high performance on the device.

To spacetime models incorporating cosmic strings, various approaches have been taken that align with the assumptions of specific theories. Our research shows, however, a direct relationship between the properties of spacetime and certain theories. A gravity-matter correlation is evident, where spacetime vorticity is linked to spinor fields' rotation.  Furthermore, electric charge conservation and spacetime vorticity are related through the spinor's degree of rotation. To generalize these connections to the spinor case, we derive the Schrodinger equation for test particles described by the Dirac equation around cosmic strings, then interpret the outcomes using the framework of spinor geometry.

A measure algebra is considered usual on a specific sigma-algebra if it is isomorphic to a subset of the measure algebra derived from the Lebesgue measure on the unit interval. The condition for being locally usual is that every generator within it is part of a larger generator that satisfies the 'usual' condition. In this paper, we present a scenario where a measurable space is constructed, featuring two probability measures such that one meets the 'locally usual' condition while the other fails to be 'usual' in a local sense. Furthermore, we establish a characterization for when the algebra generated by a partition and a 'usual' condition probability measure reduces to a sigma-finite measure algebra.

Measuring the polarization to a degree of one percent provides a precise distinction between general and specific collinear frameworks, but this measurement poses significant experimental challenges, particularly when dealing with transverse beam polarization.  We demonstrate that achieving a meaningful distinction between the gravitational form factors and the Sivers form factor in DVCS requires an initial level of beam polarization discrimination that surpasses current capabilities, thereby necessitating a highly advanced transverse polarization capable transverse-spin beam for this purpose, particularly in experiments planned at MAMI-C, JLab-CRM, LHCb, and the EIC.

Human intelligence has key strengths in creativity, ethical judgment, and processing information in an unstructured environment. Conversely, the capabilities of Artificial Intelligence are most impressive when working alone on specific tasks but often fall short when it comes to working alongside people or dealing with messy data. With the rise of collaborative efforts between humans and AI, known as Human-AI Teaming, new challenges arise in defining and understanding the knowledge and skills required for successful partnership. This study explores a new concept called Augmented Synthetic Intelligence, which involves combining advanced computer systems with more flexible and adaptive forms of knowledge and capabilities to enable them to assist humans in both professional and everyday settings. This report lays out a conceptual framework for exploring this theme, including a review of existing AI capabilities, an examination of their limitations, and a discussion of the knowledge and skills needed to support Human-AI Teaming.

Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of a spin-orbit linked superfluid of bosons that forms modulated phases in a lattice with correlated spins. By using an approach that accounts for thermal fluctuations in the many-body state of the system, specifically based on a minimum entropy principle, we have been able to gain insights into the system's behavior as it transitions from these modulated phases to ordered crystal phases as the temperature rises, finding the transition to occur at the same temperature as predicted by mean-field theory. Furthermore, our analysis reveals the influence of spin-orbit linkages on the system's dynamics at elevated temperatures, finding modulations in the superfluid velocity, local density, and order parameters to coexist in the steady state.

Graphs called "graphlets" with more than one edge have a maximum index greater than or equal to three in their source graphs, which must be abelian groups. The simplest graphlets that meet this criterion are single-edge edges. Researchers found specific classes of groups with the sole property of being realizable and determined the realizable groups within a particular subgroup, as well as the realizable group in a larger family, for any given size. The study also explored the potential for similar results in the context of graphs and their possible realizations in non-abelian groups, as well as the potential for generalization to other types of relationships in different types of structures, as hypergraphs.

Recently, it has been shown that AdS$_4$/CFT$_3$ duality can be obtained by taking a specific limit from Type IIA on $\mathbb{CP}^3$. Building upon this discovery, we examine other possible limit processes from this geometry. Our analysis reveals two more newly discovered duality models: one involving a quotient of $\mathbb{CP}^3$ and another based on $\mathbb{C} \times S^2 \times \mathbb{C} \mathbb{P}^1$.

The ability to harness the power of Gaussian process learning is significantly enhanced by developing novel kernel functions tailored to specific problems. Kernels that integrate domain and task-specific insights can lead to substantial performance gains, particularly in scenarios characterized by data scarcity. Moreover, Gaussian process kernel functions provide a flexible means of representing complex, non-parametric functions as high-dimensional linear models. As such, there is substantial potential for crafting Gaussian process kernels that incorporate insights derived from elementary mathematical expressions, such as those found in physics. This work delves into existing approaches for Gaussian process learning, including variance function estimation through maximum likelihood learning and through the use of problem-specific building blocks. By integrating these methods with building block kernels drawn from mathematical expressions, such as Gaussian processes and kernel ridge regression, it becomes possible to create Gaussian process models that effectively capture complex patterns and relationships within data.

Achieving low-precision beam separation at high-energy collider build-ups necessitates mitigating the impact of beam noise on luminosity measurements, particle interactions, and missing transverse momentum readings. This research focuses on developing strategies to mitigate beam noise in Muon Colliders and proton Colliders with high proton beam intensity. We examine relevant experiments, develop relevant detectors, and assess their efficiency in muon collider simulations using real-world examples and potential improvements and limitations.

Introducing Spartan, a novel algorithm for performing differentiated sparsification of neural networks, we utilize an optimized sparsification matrix transported from a Gaussian matrix and apply a differentiable class of entropy-based bounds. By applying gradients, the sparsification ratio can be fine-tuned during training. Experiments conducted across various architectures, including LeNet, ResNet-50, and BERT-large, demonstrate that Spartan outperforms existing methods, resulting in a well-optimized sparsification ratio.

The behavior of Bose gases at low temperatures is typically characterized by quantum Pauli blocking. In this work, we investigate the Pauli obstruction in Bose gases with low filling fractions. Our investigation relies on a perturbative combination of two theoretical approaches: the random phase approximation for calculating the excitation spectrum and the ground state energy, and the Bethe ansatz for calculating the zero sound velocity and adiabatic saturation energy. Our analysis reveals that in a weakly interacting Bose gas, the Pauli obstruction emerges when the ratio of interaction strength to filling fraction surpasses a particular numerical threshold. Moreover, we discovered that the appearance of the Pauli obstruction is accompanied by a divergent correlation length. The results of our research were verified through Monte Carlo simulations on a lattice gas and comparisons with numerical solutions to the Bethe-Salpeter equation.

Software units require comprehensive and precise coverage by their corresponding tests to ensure the reliability of the entire system. Unfortunately, developers often resort to shorthand, compact testing methods due to perceived time constraints. This paper explores the impact of such inefficient testing strategies on a developer's perspective by examining the severity of test smells from their viewpoint. The results from this study, which involved 20 participants, revealed that a lack of detailed, unit-level testing hinders a developer's ability to confidently release software, as they lose trust in its quality.

Data analysis has been significantly impacted by the development of robust statistical techniques over recent decades, with a recent emphasis on uncovering and analyzing anomalous data during the data cleaning process. A groundbreaking concept known as brushing, introduced in 1990, has been widely utilized in various fields. A novel mathematical framework has been developed to investigate the effectiveness of this data cleaning procedure, specifically focusing on a brushing process that combines convex and non-convex weighting for the purpose of cleaning data containing outliers. A new non-estimator is explored which has a consistent mean asymptotic equivalent to a trimmed mean, thereby demonstrating the applicability of this concept within outlier cleaning. Additionally, the study reveals that this non-convex weighting brushing process can efficiently eliminate outliers and has a consistent asymptotic equivalent to a trimmed mean. Furthermore, the research explores how this method can be used to prepare data before applying high-dimensional statistical techniques, such as principal component analysis, while maintaining a consistent equivalent to a trimmed covariance covariance matrix estimator.

The $e^+e^-$ collider event generator, KKMCee, is designed to create multi-photon final states up to 10 photons in intensity significantly enhanced collisions of high-energy electron and positron beams, like those of ILC, CLIC, and FCC-ee. It incorporates the effects of beam pinching and the influence of beam radiation loss upon the beam distribution into a beam group's form factor using the Monte Carlo approach. KMCee's capability is demonstrated in its interaction with the final states of $e^+e^-$ collisions at the LHCb and FCC-hh, as well as a study of the beam intensity influence and the Drell-Yan cross-section.

Measuring inter-beat intervals accurately is a critical task in diagnosing cardiovascular diseases. It's essential for both clinical and research purposes to obtain this metric, as it helps assess heart rate variability, providing valuable information about an individual's health and fitness. A paper presented at the 2022 International Multi-Confence for Clinical Engineering introduced a novel method for estimating rhythm intervals using the Tiramisu model. This method, applied to fetal heart sounds, involves a two-step process: pinpointing individual beats and estimating IBIs through regression analysis. By training on a diverse range of data, this approach outperforms conventional methods in terms of error rates and precision.

For large-scale tensor data, low-rank approximation techniques such as the singular value decomposition (SVD) and randomized algorithms have emerged as efficient methods for data compression and denoising. However, applying randomized methods to tensors often involves either a single pass or multiple passes, with trade-offs in computational efficiency and accuracy. Single-pass methods are efficient, but their accuracy is limited to certain rank approximations, while multiple passes offer improved accuracy but at a higher computational cost. This study proposes a randomized method for tensor SVD that can be adjusted to make any number of passes possible, balancing computational efficiency and accuracy. By employing a new tensor sketching algorithm based on hyperrank matrices, this method overcomes limitations of existing tensor sketching methods and allows for iterative refinement, achieving a balance between computational efficiency and accuracy in rank approximations for N-way tensors and matrices.

As various systems and applications generate continuously evolving data, graph embedding has emerged as a crucial technique for representing nodes within these networks. Traditional embedding methods, however, are limited to static graphs, whereas real-world networks are comprised of dynamic and evolving node relationships. To address this challenge, numerous methods have been proposed to address the complexity of temporal graph patterns. This paper aims to provide an in-depth analysis of these methods, comparing and evaluating existing techniques to identify advancements and improvements in these methods based on emerging applications and future research directions. Ultimately, the goal is to facilitate a comprehensive understanding of these methods and their applications to both researchers and practitioners in this field.

To investigate the structure of super- and hyper-halo nuclei, we have developed a theoretical model based on the concept of halo nuclei. Specifically, we developed a theoretical model to describe the $^7$H nucleus as a three-body system consisting of $^3$H and four neutrons, and calculated its binding energy by accounting for neutron correlations with the $^3$H cluster. Our model employs a potential function and the Monte Carlo method and reveals that weak correlations between neutrons can lead to a bound $^7$H state. Furthermore, our calculations demonstrate that strong neutron correlations can prevent the formation of a bound $^7$H state, thereby supporting the observation of a direct transition from the $^5$H resonance to the $^7$H resonance, rather than to a four-neutron resonance. Moreover, our model predicts a significant isospin symmetry breaking in the charge radii. However, our model fails to reproduce the experimentally observed charge radius of $^7$H.

We investigate the Nirenberg problem on the half unit sphere by seeking critical points of the quotient $\mathcal Q$ with respect to conformal factors, where $\mathcal Q$ measures conformal changes of the standard metric on the half sphere with a fixed boundary. It is an open question if non-trivial solutions to the Nirenberg problem exist on the half unit sphere. Utilizing a minimization method, we prove the existence of non-trivial blow-up solutions for the Nirenberg problem on the half sphere. Furthermore, we establish multiple new estimates for the function $h$ defining $\mathcal Q$, leveraging these estimates to provide the first demonstration of non-trivial blow-up solutions for the Nirenberg problem on half spheres.

Deep learning models significantly outperform previous approaches in representation learning tasks, but their ability to achieve optimal representations is often compromised when working with limited datasets. In contrast, traditional methods utilizing explicit feature representations can accomplish this optimality. Our investigation delves into the possibility of imparting deep networks with a sophisticated yet interpretable set of constraints capable of directing learning toward more effective representations. These constraints utilize pairwise cross-domain losses calculated via OT, known as Sinkhorn losses, forming the foundation of our approach known as Deep OT. Our research reveals that OT serves as a form of dimensionality reduction and can be interpreted as a form of self-supervision. Moreover, the effectiveness of our Deep OT framework relies on the choice of OT kernel parameters, which can be understood in terms of a deep generalization landscape. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that Deep OT surpasses all previous approaches in representation learning tasks on various datasets, comprising both real and synthetic data.

This research examines how local public health efforts to track and contain COVID-19 cases in England have influenced the overall effectiveness of contact tracing. The study uses an established mathematical model to simulate the interactions between various local tracing programs. The results indicate that local variations in case tracking and follow-up rates have significant implications for the success of contact tracing, a factor that the national system of data collection and sharing fails to capture adequately. The data from one local area, known as 'Area A,' shows that case reporting to the national system underestimates the actual number of cases by approximately 10%, resulting in follow-up rates around 40% and a lower number of infected contacts traced than in areas with higher national follow-up rates. The national system's reliance on data reported by local authorities to schedule test and trace appointments, combined with delays and data entry issues, contributes to this underestimation. The national policy of allowing only a small percentage of high-risk cases to be traced is another limiting factor for the success of contact tracing, particularly in areas with lower local tracing efficiency. The study suggests that improving data collection and processing by local authorities and adjusting national policies to prioritize tracing high-risk cases could significantly boost the success of contact tracing, potentially reducing the number of COVID-19 cases generated by infected contacts and bringing the basic reproductive number ($R_0$) below 2.

Preliminary data from the Gaia mission indicate that the cluster, Melotte 72, may be categorized as an "intermediate age" cluster.  Although Melotte 72 has been a subject of study for its physical properties, its current classification as an "intermediate age" cluster presents difficulties in using isochrone fitting methods due to its ambiguous position.  Our research employs data from the Gaia DR2 to determine key properties of Melotte 72 and to compare its structure to other well-studied clusters.  Our analysis includes processing the Gaia DR2 data to generate color-magnitude diagrams (CMDs) and determining its radial velocity, mass, and distance by cross-referencing data from existing studies.  By applying photometric corrections to the Gaia DR2 data, we are able to produce CMDs that reveal a main sequence turn-off (MSTO) consistent with a main sequence broadening and the Gaia parallax.  Our findings reveal a mass of $0.742\pm0.013$ times that of the sun and a distance of $177\pm10$ parsecs from the sun.  Our research also reveals a notable main sequence broadening and a possible evidence of a main sequence split and a tail of blue stars in the cluster.  By comparing our results with other "intermediate age" and subgroups of clusters, we are able to identify a pattern of group

This study investigates the distribution of Betti numbers in the kth homology group of a complex known as the Gaussian k-plex. We focus particularly on the regime where the edge probability $p$ approaches the critical point $1 - \frac{k}{2n}$ from below as $n$ approaches infinity. Our main finding reveals that, almost certainly, the expected number of Betti elements behaves asymptotically like $\binom{n}{k+1}p^{k+1}$. This result is achieved by first establishing an upper limit, which involves showing that the number of relevant k-plexes does not significantly deviate from its mean, and then leveraging this fact to derive a probabilistic bound for the total number of k-Betti elements based on their maximum possible size.

This paper investigates adjusting the parameters of an eye-in-hand camera due to misalignment or imperfections in its intrinsic properties. We introduce a technique that infers the parameters of both rotation and intrinsic adjustments from a singular image with an embedded embedded homography representation. Our proposed method, based on neural networks, involves training the camera's parameters by randomizing them during a data enhancement process. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in tackling misalignment and intrinsic calibration issues.

In reinforcement learning scenarios, sometimes there are unanticipated adverse effects that need to be avoided at a minimum, for which we have established a set of required targets in reverse constrained reinforcement learning. We introduce a new framework for this problem, employing contrastive rewards and a reversed Bellman equation in off-policy value estimation. However, our methods are limited to low-density high values of action space, which hampers sample efficiency. We overcome this limitation by developing a novel approach utilizing partial supervision and integrating the Fenchel-Yosida subdifferential operator into value regression.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission is set to significantly advance our understanding of the Galaxy and its star populations by submitting over 10 billion source candidates for final data release 3 in 2023. To maximize GAIA's impact, scientists are leveraging novel approaches to model the Galaxy using the provided dataset, thereby unlocking diverse scientific insights across a broad spectrum. Researchers are applying unique machine learning tools to GAIA data, enabling more precise execution of traditional methods. In this article, we explore current machine learning applications in Galaxy research, including substructure detection, star formation modeling, star formation rate estimation, star formation age estimation, star formation site identification, star formation event identification, star formation event classification, binary star detection, and binary star classification. To facilitate this exploration, the article also covers machine learning fundamentals, including dataset preparation, feature engineering, model evaluation, and model optimization. Future research directions and challenges are outlined, along with a comprehensive summary of the GAIA mission's planned data releases.

For any graph with treewidth $d$, we present linear-time algorithms to create a partition into sets of size at most $n/2$ with no more than $O(d\log d + n)$ edges across the partitions. Achieving similar algorithms with a bounded number of edges requires $O(n)$ vertices. Notably, these new algorithms significantly enhance the existing best algorithms by a polynomial factor in terms of $d$, while maintaining substantial space efficiency. A crucial part of our design is an algorithmically efficient and widely applicable process for generating short list of random numbers with a uniform distribution using $O(\log n)$ bits.

We introduce the concept of weighted grouping in the context of networks, focusing on its definition, interpretation, and implications for social and biological systems. We recognize that groupings can be diverse in nature, ranging from pre-defined categories to data-driven clusters inferred from structural, semantic, or mixed connections. We explore the meaning of weights in groupings and how they can reflect various levels of strength, confidence levels, or time-based intensities. We also outline three distinct types of groupings - structural, semantic, and temporal - highlighting their unique characteristics and applications.

For each type of grouping, we outline the specific requirements to make weighted grouping useful, ensuring the validity of the analysis. We then introduce the Weighted Directed Grouping (WDG) measure as a framework for joint interpretation of networks and groupings, emphasizing its significance in the analysis of groupings. We apply both warded and joint interpretations to a range of networks and demonstrate how WDG can uncover hidden relationships in those networks, such as a strong tie between a weak tie and other strong ties in a network.

Physics-informed neural networks have emerged as a promising method for solving partial differential equations with embedded physical constraints. However, these networks can be misused if not properly validated, potentially leading to incorrect solutions and false expectations. To address this issue, we propose a new approach called certified error estimation that quantifies the error of PINNs without relying on assumptions. This technique involves analyzing the maximum error over a domain and subdomains, and we implement it for the Poisson equation in various scenarios. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and its ability to verify PINN results.

In recent years, an increasing number of epidemiological studies have focused on the effects of air pollution on human health, with research areas including the respiratory and cardiovascular systems, as well as cognitive function and other conditions.  Analyzing and predicting spatio-temporal air pollution patterns poses a complex challenge due to multiple factors, such as varying pollution sources and patterns, and significant changes in patterns over different time scales.  Given the multi-dimensional and high-noise characteristics of available data, developing efficient and accurate pollution models poses a particular challenge.  Filling this knowledge gap is essential for policymakers to establish effective guidelines, with various proposed solutions drawing from traditional and cutting-edge machine learning approaches.  This article aims to provide an up-to-date review of air pollution modeling methods in epidemiology studies, with a particular focus on the application of geostatistical and machine learning techniques.

Our computational investigation focuses on tunneling spectroscopy measurements for identifying Majorana modes within topological superconductors, specifically those with an ohmic dissipative barrier. This barrier arises from an intermediate layer between the superconductor and quantum dot that lacks no relevant energy scale, in contrast to previous studies assuming an isolated Majorana potential. Our results show distinct asymmetries between the tunneling spectra of left and right contacts, which provide clear signatures to differentiate the Majorana peak from other peaks corresponding to quantum dot energy levels, even in the presence of minor model parameter variations. This research aims to establish reliable, non-ambiguous topological spectroscopy protocols beyond the idealized scenarios.

We examine a linear reward bandit problem with a wealth of possible actions, where it's demonstrated that with a constant factor regret it's feasible to find an approximate maximizer of the linear regression problem acting as its underlying model. This regression's covariance matrix comprises at most polynomial values with respect to its dimension, ensuring its inverse can effectively influence a constant-regret algorithm's performance. Crucially, our proof relies on a matrix influence argument that might be useful in other learning contexts, ultimately allowing us to show that a polynomial-time algorithm can achieve a constant factor in the best possible regret performance.

Graphene with gaps has the potential to exhibit the orbital valley Hall effect in the presence of an impulsive disorder, which can be controlled by adjusting the strength of magnetic fields, monolayer arrangements, and Bernal stacking graphs. Introducing a disorder pulse affects the valley electrons without impacting orbital currents, resulting in the orbital Hall effect when magnetic fields are applied. Notably, the orbital Hall effect's efficiency surpasses that of impulsive disorder by one order of magnitude, and it can be controlled by varying the magnetic field strength. When a field strength of 50 T is applied, this effect becomes comparable to the Chern-Simons value in graphene strips of 100 nm width.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective across various graph-related tasks. Like other network models, GNNs are susceptible to data manipulation attacks, presenting a novel category of adversarial threats known as data contamination attacks. These threats arise when an attacker modifies the training data to hinder GNN performance. While traditional data contamination attacks typically involve random noise, we introduce the concept of node-based data manipulation tailored specifically for GNNs. A GRL approach is developed to tackle this issue, leveraging reinforcement learning to optimize the对抗性对抗策略, achieved through the creation of a GRL framework consisting of a value network and a policy network. Experimental outcomes showcase the efficacy of this GRL approach in inducing significant performance drops on GNNs both in induced and traditional node-based data manipulation scenarios.

Creating a match between two star catalogs involves identifying unique objects across these sources. To optimize this process, we developed a novel approach that incorporates both astrometric and photometric data, generating predicted position movements and brightness levels for two catalogs as evidence to support our algorithm. To test its effectiveness, we processed both synthetic datasets and a real-world application, comparing the results against standard catalog-based matches, ultimately showcasing the potential benefits of integrating multi-wavelength astrometric and photometric data to enhance matching accuracy.

We establish a minimum requirement for the cardinality of a set $X$ in an infinite $(k,r)$-uniform hypergraph, such that removing $X$ results in fewer than $\mathcal{L}$ edges. Specifically, if the remaining edge size is less than $r$, then the minimum size of $X$ must satisfy $|X| \geq \Theta_{\mathcal{L}}(M(\kappa,\mathcal{L},r,k))^{(r-1)/(r-2)}$, where $M(\kappa,\mathcal{L},r,k)$ is a constant determined by the values of $\mathcal{L}$, $r $, and $k $. This lower bound holds for all $\mathcal{L} > 1 $, and our work further shows that this bound cannot be exceeded by a factor that grows with the size of the hypergraph index $m $. Instead, the upper bound grows as $O_m(\Delta^{k-2}) $, where $\Delta $ is the maximum degree of the hypergraph, and we demonstrate this result by constructing $m$-uniform $(k,r)$-hypergraphs containing $\mathcal{L}$ edges of size at least $r $, and a set $X$ such that removing $X $ leaves an edge size no greater than $|\mathit{E}| - \Omega(m\Delta^{k-2}) $.

Ontologies, essential for data exchange in ontological approaches, enable various applications across data-driven industries. However, their applicability is hindered by the limited data visualization techniques available, many of which apply to small datasets or utilize generic graph visualization methods, producing unsatisfactory results. Our solution, OntoPlot, is a visualization tool specifically designed for ontopology associations, showcasing numerous innovations. By employing a unique encoding method for color, size, and shape of graph elements, and a novel plotting technique for visualizing circular data distributions, and a novel navigation method for navigating large-scale ontopologies, and novel filtering technique for focusing on specific subsets of the graph. Our evaluation of OntoPlot reveals its exceptional capabilities in clarity, readability, and ease of use compared to generic graph visualization techniques, supported by user tests and comparisons with a leading ontology visualization tool.

We've successfully applied CycleGAN and introduced an innovative loss function to increase data diversity across domains without requiring labels in their original settings. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to end-to-end Automatic Speech Recognition models. By expanding training set variety, cycle-consistency and fine tuning losses significantly improve the recognition accuracy on speakers from different domains, as opposed to models without these additional losses. Specifically, the system's performance is enhanced in scenarios where the speakers in the source domain originate from a different environment, like a different location or a different time period, compared to speakers who simply use various accents or speak in distinct emotional tones. These latest findings are encapsulated by Confluent et al. on the latest benchmark.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to active navigation called Deep Active Prediction (DAP). DAP relies on a neural network-based simulator and path planning to enable a robot to collect the most informative data for map learning. In each step, the method evaluates potential actions using the open-loop advanced simulator, which offers a significant speed advantage over closed-loop simulations. Furthermore, it incorporates a novel, fast heuristic to identify structure changes in potential views, which are critical for map learning. DAP also prioritizes exploring uncharted areas. Experimental results demonstrate that DAP results in simulators with higher information content, more complete structures, and their 3D counterparts show comparable performance on a real autonomous robot navigating an indoor environment.

This study uses molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the thermal diffusion of molecules with flexible structures. Notably, our findings reveal that these molecules exhibit a weaker Soret effect compared to those with rigid structures. A key factor influencing this observation is identified as an increased internal entropy associated with higher flexibilities, facilitating a state of higher entropy at negative temperature gradients. Building on this insight, a theoretical model accurately predicts the thermal diffusion coefficient of flexible molecules. Validated through simulations, our framework reveals that a molecule's flexibility significantly impacts its thermal diffusion. These findings have important implications for understanding phenomena such as esters in crude oil and polymeric additives in lubricants under temperature gradients.

Automated essay scoring has gained significant attention in the Natural Language Processing community. Our research enhances the performance of External Reader models for automated essay assessment by optimizing the Transformer architecture. We introduce two innovative approaches - Sparse and Pruned Transformers - which reduce the computational complexity of Transformer ascribed networks without compromising scoring accuracy. We utilized our model on Development ASSET data, comparing it against 9 features with Singlehead DQN Q-Learning. The Pruned Transformer achieved the highest precision, surpassing our model's performance by achieving a Precision of 0.77, followed by our head sparsed Precison of 0.74, finally our head sparsed and weight pruned Precision of 0.73.

Deep learning-based object detectors have achieved remarkable success in numerous applications, yet a persistent issue of high false positive rates in underrepresented areas continues to be a significant challenge. Although researchers have made considerable progress in reducing false positives through annotation reduction techniques, the problem still plagues these detectors. One application heavily affected by this issue is pedestrian detection, as cameras often capture a variety of objects, making distinguishing pedestrians from similar objects like statues or mannequins difficult. We introduce a straightforward and efficient technique for re-ordering predicted boxes in order to significantly reduce false positives in pedestrian detection tasks without requiring costly manual annotation. The proposed approach involves training a model on the most probable false positives to better differentiate between them and then applying it to the predicted boxes. We conducted comprehensive evaluations on benchmark datasets, including Sunflower, Cityflows, BDD100K, and nuWaves, revealing that our proposed method results in a substantial decrease in false positives while retaining high recall rates. We surprisingly find that our technique works even in fully supervised settings and performs comparably in self-supervised contexts.

We propose an end-to-end approach to enhancing low-quality audio files, such as those with poor sound quality from phone recordings, by using deep learning techniques. To address the problem of unknown noise characteristics, we employ a generalised transformation learned from data. Using LibRIssl as a high-quality reference, we employ style transfer and noise suppression techniques to clean up the audio. Finally, we apply a vocoder to further enhance the sound quality. Our method yields a significant intelligibility improvement when compared to the original audio and outperforms state-of-the-art noise cancellation and speech denoising techniques in challenges like Google's Speech Denoising Challenge.

Our research, FauxThrow, examines how artificial anomalies in object release points affect human arm trajectory planning during throwing. By analyzing real-world throwing data, we discovered distinct pointing movements that indicate release points and found this to be a consistent feature across various throwing scenarios.
